Our research builds upon this concept by adapting a novel image generation method, known as Latent Class Generative Adversarial Networks (LCGAN), to tackle the complex task of colorizing monochrome satellite images. To address the uniqueness constraints inherent in remote sensing data sets, we incorporated a total variation (TV) loss function into our model's optimization process. Furthermore, our results reveal the efficacy of leveraging an image fusion-based approach to calculate the output signal for the discriminator. To substantiate the superiority of our LCGAN-based method, we conducted a comprehensive comparison of its performance against three rival network architectures.

We introduce a novel neural network architecture, termed GFNN, which is rooted in the Universal Approximation Theorem. This approach bypasses the conventional gradient-based optimization in backpropagation, instead relying on a straightforward propagation mechanism to achieve similar performance. Our results demonstrate that GFNN accurately replicates the behavior of a standard multilayer perceptron, including input-output mapping and error calculation. Additionally, we found that GFNN's weight updating process in a fully connected network aligns with that of a neural network trained using stochastic gradient descent. Notably, GFNN offers enhanced computational efficiency and enhanced robustness to hyperparameter selection. Our findings are substantiated by exhaustive numerical experiments across diverse scenarios.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRDC) plays a vital role in representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA framework. Established in 2021 to enhance involvement of early career researchers (ECRs) in ECFA's activities and decision-making processes, the committee has made significant progress in its first two years of operation. This report outlines the committee's purpose, composition, organizational structure, and key actions taken during its initial term.

Recent advancements have brought quantum meetspace technology into the optical realm, led by dual metasurfaces that merge nonreciprocal radiation characteristics with optical principles. A crucial feature of these metasurfaces is their ability to control the direction of radiation, properties that are heavily dependent on the concept of momentum. However, this momentum's relationship is significantly altered when dealing with optical impects. This unique association enables novel capabilities such as controlling optical ripples along a line, creating optical droponium, and managing optical mode directional radiation. Despite the potential of these capabilities, the existing research has largely focused on the inherent nonlocality of dual metasurfaces, neglecting their inherent momentum structure's significance. This paper seeks to clarify this critical aspect by introducing a theoretical framework that illustrates how the momentum's direction can influence optical ripples and directional radiation phenomena. Using dual fishnet structures, we demonstrate the framework's practical application, showcasing our ability to customize optical ripples and mode directional radiation. Ultimately, this research aims to inspire the development of cutting-edge optical devices leveraging the momentum's direction, paving the way for innovative optical technology advancements.

Effective training cognitive AI agents requires extensive data and is best achieved through prolonged, specially designed learning programs. The advent of collaborative learning between humans and robots offers a promising approach, as it allows for distributed, cost-effective, and efficient learning. Prior research has primarily focused on theoretical aspects and has yet to fully implement a scalable architecture for practical use. This work introduces a comprehensive, open-source cognitive architecture that supports multi-agent collaborative learning among large numbers of humans and robots. The architecture's key features include a dynamic task management system capable of handling numerous learning tasks, a unified data management system facilitating seamless data sharing among agents, and a adaptable decision-making mechanism enabling agents to choose from multiple learning strategies. To test this architecture, a cross-disciplinary project involving researchers in cognitive AI, learning technologies, and social networks was conducted, utilizing virtual reality to create a distributed learning environment involving human-robot collaborations. The results demonstrated the architecture's ability to effectively manage complex learning environments and suggested that optimized parameter settings can yield comparable results to expert-designed models.

To account for the downward bias of the mean absolute deviation (MAD) from the median, three modified estimators are proposed, incorporating continuity corrections established in the literature. These corrections address the findings of Elting et al. (2021) and are further refined to ensure asymptotic normality, a property previously identified by Kozabu Matsuchi (2020) for the classic MAD estimator. Our novel estimators maintain the same consistency and have a rate of convergence as the classic MAD estimator, as shown by Kozabu Matsuchi (2020). Additionally, two bias-corrected estimators proposed in this study outperform the classic MAD estimator in terms of asymptotic normality and its associated properties. The behavior of these estimators is evaluated through extensive simulation studies and applied to actual data from two real-world studies.

The primary goal of relation extraction is to identify and categorize the relationship between two key entities within a text passage.  Achieving high precision in this task is challenging because human annotators often disagree on the relationships between text-based entities.  To address this challenge, our approach utilizes knowledge graph link prediction to refine relation extraction by utilizing additional knowledge graph data.  By incorporating knowledge graph information, our model can make more accurate predictions than a baseline method that only utilizes text data, and it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in precision and F1 score on the Benchmark of Automatic Relation Identification dataset.

The behavior of anisotropic flows for various quarkonium states as a function of binding energy has been examined, and key observations were made regarding their dissociation characteristics in a non-uniform, momentum-anisotropic Quark-Gluon Plasma environment. Notably, for the most stably bound quarkonium states, the momentum-anisotropy has a relatively minimal effect on their dissociation properties, but further research into their physical implications is still needed. Additionally, when considering finite baryonic chemical potential, the Debye mass increases in accordance with quasi-particle theory, resulting in the dissociation temperature rising in line with binding energy for quarkonia.

Recent studies on Ru chain compounds exhibit unique magnetic properties. Specifically, the internal magnetic fields created by neighboring spins in these chains significantly affect their magnetic behaviors. To further explore this phenomenon, researchers examined the magnetic characteristics of the natural tetragonal crystal growth plane (110), particularly at very low temperatures, using a high magnetic field aligned with the [001] direction. They discovered that the Ru ions within this compound adopt a half-integer spin state of 1/2, contrary to initial expectations of a 0-integer spin state. By applying a substantial external magnetic field, the Ru ions transition into a 0-integer spin state of 0. The unique magnetic configurations of the Tb ions in this compound also play a crucial role in shaping its magnetic properties. The unique internal magnetic fields created by the 8-fold coordinated Tb ions substantially influence the magnetic behaviors, resulting in an exceptionally disordered magnetic state at very low temperatures when exposed to a low external magnetic field.

While generative visualizations are widely employed to ensure transparent model decisions, they often fall short due to overly simplistic results. We introduce the Modulated Periodic Activation (MPA) layer, a flexible and modular design that bridges the gap between detailed internal representations and visually appealing outputs. We utilize low-frequency activations to highlight key features in functional MRI, low-resolution images, and 3D medical scans, ultimately demonstrating improved visualizations over existing methods. Additionally, our model enhances the interpretability of neural networks by producing actionable illustrations. We showcase the efficacy of the MPA layer in our repository, including accompanying technical details in the supplementary section.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adjustment can be ineffective in practical scenarios.  We're introducing Semi-Generative Modelling (SGM), a novel framework that effectively handles cases with cause and effect features in such scenarios.  By combining importance sampling with synthetic data generation, SGM enhances the capacity of models to adapt to shifting distributions.  We've developed a specific algorithm to implement SGM, demonstrating its superiority over existing techniques in experimental studies.

Deep neural networks have achieved impressive results, yet the intricacies of their workings remain poorly understood. By examining the geometric properties of deep learning, we gain insight into the fundamental mechanisms governing neural network behavior. This insight enables us to derive a unified framework that seamlessly integrates various deep learning methods, striking a balance between mathematical rigor and intuitive clarity. Key concepts such as chain rule, Hessian matrix, and Jacobian matrix are reinterpreted to illuminate their significance in backpropagation and error backpropagation. Furthermore, we explore the implications of Taylor expansion and expectation propagation on learning dynamics and demonstrate the connection between different deep learning methods through invariant analysis.

One of the main factors of an algebraic torus $T$ can be viewed as a subgroup of the lattice of rational character lattices $\Lambda$. We establish that the ideal of $\Lambda$ generated by its main factors has a crucial property: it is comprised of elements whose corresponding central simple algebra laminations have an embedding variety of reduced dimension. We prove that this result holds for arbitrary algebraic tori, without being restricted to split tori or tori defined over local fields. Additionally, for tori over a local field, we determine the precise lattice minima, demonstrating that they form a group under multiplication and infimum under the $2$-norm, and showing that their intersection with positive character lattices yields a subgroup with a crucial property when combined with the ideal generated by lattice minima of algebraic tori.

A key role in particle physics is played by machine learning algorithms known as deep neural network jet taggers, which are used to identify and analyze hadron jets produced by high-energy particle collisions. In this study, we provide insights into the decision-making processes of these deep neural network taggers through the use of expert variables and a novel interpretation method called Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation. Our analysis reveals that despite achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art deep neural network taggers, simpler models fared poorly in jet tagging tasks, highlighting the complexity of these tasks and the need for highly refined models. Additionally, we find that the most influential inputs to deep neural network taggers are often located at the base of the network, and that these models are highly resistant to perturbations.

For every positive integer n, consider the set Sr(n) of all the reflections related to the signed permutations of n. Specifically, a reflection is a swap of two adjacent elements followed by an option to change the sign of the swapped element. Given this context, the total count of these reflections, denoted as $|{\mathfrak R}(n)|$, can be expressed as an extension of the Stirling numbers of the first kind, specifically $|{\mathfrak R}(n)| = 2^{n}r_{n}$ where $r_{n}$ represents the Stirling number of the first kind. This paper aims to provide a generalized version of the degenerate r-related Stirling numbers, denoted as $r_{(m,n)}(x)$, and derive closed-form expressions for the generating functions of two distinct varieties of these degenerate Stirling numbers: those without a signed component and those with a signed component. For the former, the results align with the principles of Eggleton; for the latter, the results are a degenerate extension of the signed Stirling numbers of the first kind, as introduced by Chotai and Hsu.

The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the irreducible and site-symmetry induced representations for bragg strata surrounding high-symmetry points within the Brillouin zone of a hexagonal lattice. Specifically, the study focuses on double, single ordinary, and double gray layers adjacent to A, M, R, and K high-symmetry points. By combining the properties of layer groups and Wyckoff sites, the research lists site-symmetry induced irreducible modules for all strata using a standardized notation that reflects the geometric relationships within these layers. Additionally, the paper outlines methods for constructing physical properties through the combination of lower-dimensional irrep sets, providing essential tools for investigating dynamic phenomena in 2D heterostructures.

For a spacetime with Killing vector fields, the integral curves of which are geodesics, we examine the Lie algebra structure and the commutator properties of the momentum operators. We derive conditions under which the Lie algebra of such momentum operators lies in a specific form, such as abelian, simple, or semisimple, based on the characteristics of the Killing vector fields and their flow. This research also explores the implications for systems with finite degrees of freedom and discusses the consequences for the eigenvalue spectra of such systems.

A novel implementation of neural networks that utilizes complex numbers instead of the traditional real number method has been proposed to mitigate the Hubbard sign problem. This new approach called cNNs is capable of modeling complex probability amplitudes by leveraging complex propagators and wavefunctions. By doing so, it can tackle challenging quantum systems without relying on imaginary time evolution methods. Furthermore, this framework has shown promising cross-domain generalization capabilities. Experiments on simple quantum systems have yielded accurate results and even achieved better performance compared to real number networks. However, it is expected that its computational cost will increase exponentially for larger systems.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, we propose an idea in which the flavon, a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, is linked to a $U(1) \rightarrow U(1)'$ symmetry breaking. This flavon, which acquires a VEV, causes a similar pattern in a separate $SU(5)$ theory, resulting in the diminishment of third-generation Yukawa coupling constants. To verify the feasibility of this concept, we'll demonstrate the possibility of accurately setting the scale of flavon mass by properly selecting the mass of an additional vector boson produced in the $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ theory. Additionally, this model offers an explanation for the disparity between the first two families and the third, ultimately leading to a natural outcome for the third-generation Yukawa constants.

User experiences in Virtual-Reality (VR) can be enhanced through perceptual distortions, which offer various advantages but also pose potential risks to user safety and well-being. Current research largely focuses on the benefits, disregarding the concealed hazards. This paper reveals the hidden perils of VR experiences, incorporating research findings on spatial disorientation, navigation confusions, and anxiety/procrastination induced by stereoscopic vision. The research emphasizes the necessity of balancing VR benefits with user safety limits and suggests establishing clear guidelines for responsible VR application development.

To assess various architectures' and adaptation methods' effectiveness for unrelated languages, we introduce a unified, unmodified, and zero-shot translation setup within the BigScience large-scale multilingual model. Our results reveal that a combination of translation direction and additional data influences zero-shot translation performance, whereas other factors have minimal impact. Furthermore, we identify potential issues with the zero-shot translation feature in the BigScience model, as observed in our experiments, and suggest several areas for further investigation.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of binary systems. Their data have shown mass ratios and orbital periods that match computer simulations precisely. These simulations start with a parent core that undergoes fragmentation due to rotational instability. The total mass of this core increases over time, and the binary characteristics formed from its breakdown closely resemble the observations. This process can create masses for each binary component that aligns with the data. Furthermore, all resulting binary masses have been compared with the masses of run-away stars that were once part of a binary system that dissolved. Their distribution patterns also match the computer simulations that model binary creation.

This research introduces the M-ar-K-Fast version of the Autonomous Component Analysis algorithm, an efficient tool for analyzing complex data sets. The M-ar-K-Fast algorithm is an optimization method that emerges from a novel variant of the Autonomous Component Analysis algorithm. This variant incorporates a non-convex error function and active sets optimization to reduce its computational cost. The M-ar-K-Fast algorithm is now faster, more resilient to local minima, and less sensitive to initial condition choices. Furthermore, this algorithm's error function is related to the total sum of the absolute deviations, making it a useful tool for statistical analysis. The M-ar-K-Fast algorithm outperforms other versions of the algorithm in finding optimal solutions, particularly for large data sets. Examples of its effectiveness can be found in applications like financial risk assessment, the analysis of the distribution of prices across time, and the study of the distribution of prices when repeated measurements are available.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It focuses on pinpointing which theoretical framework best captures the computational power of a particular class of finite models. This investigation also makes a proof a priori more transparent by translating it into a more visual framework. Additionally, the study related to choiceless polynomial calculus reveals a limitation on the depth of distinguishability of graph properties that is inherent, thereby implying a related lower bound on the depth of refutations in the polynomial calculus. A comparable lower bound for Extended Polynomial Calculus has also been discovered. Furthermore, a novel way of constructing hardness reductions has been introduced, which is based on a specific type of extension to choiceless polynomial calculus. This type of reduction is capable of maintaining parameters such as depth, degree, and clause size within predetermined bounds. Such a reduction has not been constructed before, and it is anticipated that it will have far-reaching applications.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor uncommutative, is defined as being $\sigma$-nil, $\sigma$-prime, $\sigma$-composite or $\sigma$-elementary with respect to a given set $\sigma$. Endless sets of rings that are respectively $\sigma$-nil, $\sigma$-prime, $\sigma$-composite or $\sigma$-elementary are now presented. It is demonstrated that a ring $R$ is $\sigma$-elementary if and only if $R$ is $\sigma$-nil and $\sigma$-prime. Furthermore, it has been found that a ring $R$ is $\sigma$-elementary if and only if $R \cong S \times T$ where $S$ and $T$ are commutative rings from the set $\sigma$.

Social media platforms are contending with a significant problem of spread unfalsifiable claims that cause harm to users. A claim is deemed unfalsifiable if no evidence can be gathered to contradict it. Our research introduces the concept of a truth assessment framework, which enables evaluating the reliability of claims by gathering different types of evidence. We acknowledge that current information assessment methods on social media are inadequate and develop a method to locate a suitable framework through data analysis. Our approach, which combines statistical analysis and machine learning, identifies a framework that excels in accurate truth-assessment by leveraging a large dataset of claims gathered from fact-checking organizations. We also recognize the challenges associated with choosing the most suitable framework, including the need for more data sharing among fact-checking organizations and the incorporation of additional information such as the level of agreement among fact-checkers.

Identifying incidents in real-time from social media is crucial for swift and effective response strategies. Current methods for incident detection on social media are hampered by challenges such as ambiguity in user posts and delayed detection due to time discrepancies. To address these issues, we have developed a robust framework for real-time spatio-temporal incident detection on social media. This innovative method incorporates a novel algorithm that leverages concurrent anomalous pattern recognition and user post analysis to accurately pinpoint incidents. Furthermore, our framework precisely aligns social media posts with a road network using a geospatial mapping technique, resolving the ambiguity problem and enabling location-specific incident detection. This method also utilizes user-generated content and social media user profiles to verify detected incidents and enhance accuracy. In addition, our framework incorporates a module that identifies and filters out false positives. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's capability to detect incidents concurrently and accurately locate them geographically, thereby overcoming key limitations of social media-based incident detection methods.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We've developed a rapid method for CMB lensing bispectrum analysis by leveraging existing techniques and computational resources to simplify the process. Compared to the standard approach, our method significantly reduces computational requirements, achieving a speedup of about 100 times. We've verified the accuracy and flexibility of our method in several tests. We've also refined our algorithm to extract accurate bispectrum signals from realistic data by applying cross-correlation analysis on the CMB lensing and galaxy surveys combination, while removing large-scale effects. The technique's limitations stem from its reliance on quadrupole moment approximation and potential foreground contamination, along with data quality and noise levels. We've demonstrated the method's effectiveness on the CMB and galaxy surveys combination through $t$-test, and outlined a straightforward strategy for bias correction. The technique's potential applications include the CMB and galaxy surveys combination, as well as other datasets such as CMB-pol and spectroscopic galaxy surveys.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep networks, we can develop robust models capable of handling complex attacks. However, current methods based on variational inference fail when confronted with data in the form of a set of examples. In contrast, our proposed Bayesian training approach, which we term 'Bayesian Adversarial Learning with Sampling' (BALS), successfully combines Bayesian and adversarial training. To accomplish this, BALS employs a sampling-based method for approximating the posterior distribution, thereby avoiding the pitfalls associated with approximations via stochastic gradient variational inference. As a result, BALS provides verifiable robustness guarantees and outperforms alternative methods on standard machine learning benchmarks.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we introduced two novel metrics: the diffusion speed and impact of rumors, which enabled the creation of an efficient algorithm for identifying and ranking high-spreading risks. Furthermore, we proposed a rumor influence measurement method grounded in centrality analysis and clustering validation metrics. Our study, focused on China's most popular social media platform Weibo, selected 119 critical instances of online rumors surrounding the pandemic. By applying the developed metrics, we evaluated the diffusion process and assessed the effectiveness of countermeasures implemented by Weibo and official authorities. Our empirical results confirmed the accuracy and practical value of the proposed metrics, which could be extended to monitoring and predicting online rumors in other crisis situations.

This study investigated the effects of applying different spectral dimensionality reduction methods to high-resolution hyperspectral images, and assessed their impact on pixel classification in a real-world context. Three methods - Principal Component Analysis, Autoencoders, and t-Distributed Negative Point Map - were used to reduce the spectral dimensions of 100 hyperspectral images, resulting in improved classification accuracy according to the used criteria. Interestingly, the study found that while these methods enhanced the computational efficiency of classification models, they also had a negative impact on accuracy, with the worst results observed for images with limited spectral diversity. Furthermore, the study discovered that a combination of reduced spatial and spectral dimensions led to the most notable decline in classification accuracy. Based on the findings, the study concludes that dimensionality reduction should be carefully considered before classification, and that the choice of method depends on the characteristics of images and the desired classification outcome.

Recent research has demonstrated the efficacy of text compression methods in enhancing the robustness and performance of text classifiers by filtering out harmful data examples. Although the existing literature mainly focuses on the compression of anomalous data, this work investigates the effectiveness of compressing clean text examples to eliminate data duplicates and potentially improve model robustness. Our research reveals that compressing text data yields distinct benefits to classification robustness and model generalization capabilities. Moreover, we discovered that the most advantageous compression approaches tend to produce longer compressed sequences than those that enhance robustness, highlighting a trade-off between generalization and error reduction. To further explore the implications of text compression, we proposed two novel metrics designed to evaluate the effect of compression on authentic data, in addition to proposing several promising directions for future research.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, has been developed to accurately predict the chemical shifts of protein amide protons. This prediction is based on quantum mechanical calculations of the proton-electron spin interaction, taking into consideration the fast motion of water in the protein's surroundings, as influenced by the dynamic properties of protein structures. ProCS achieves an error margin of less than 0.3 ppm for the prediction of amide proton chemical shifts, thereby enabling it to supplement existing prediction methods, which have a larger margin of error. Furthermore, ProCS is capable of differentiating between correct and incorrect protein structures, with a success rate of around 80% in validating protein structures, and also demonstrates the ability to refine protein structures through energy minimization, resulting in a 20% improvement based on energy calculations.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a crucial decision with far-reaching implications, yet the extent to which different loss functions influence model behavior and data augmentation remains poorly understood. In this study, we examine how loss functions affect image classification models when applied to two different datasets, considering various factors including global optimization trends, model architecture, dataset characteristics, and residual camera images. Our analysis reveals that loss function selection can render certain pre-trained models ineffective, underscoring the need for a comprehensive understanding of its implications in deep learning applications.

Based on Kadanoff-Baym equations, a perturbative parquet theory is developed to track higher-order particle-hole and particle-particle irreducible vertices. By transforming these vertices into corresponding effective actions and verifying their closure, the theory is validated at each order. Furthermore, the parquet theory is formulated in terms of Hamiltonians that encapsulate all non-linear effects, offering an alternative perspective on the subject.

Using a reliable approach that incorporates density-functional theory and continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo, we've investigated the dynamical phase transition to exciton condensation in $n$-doped 1$H$-$TiSe_2$. By systematically examining the structural and spectral changes during the condensation process, we've observed that the system undergoes significant transformations which are consistent with an initial increase in electron-phonon coupling that triggers a soft mode instability. However, at high doping levels the influence of electron-phonon coupling rapidly diminishes and the rise of exciton-like surface states becomes the primary driver of the exciton condensation process, which is a characteristic feature of superconductors. Furthermore, using a reliable technique for calculating many-body spectral weight, we've quantitatively evaluated the doping-level-dependent strength of electron-photon interaction and obtained results which are in excellent agreement with the findings from x-ray spectroscopy. We've also shown that the technique used to analyze the condensation process is highly versatile and can be applied to a broad range of materials and their unique behaviors under different external influences.

In areas with limited infrastructure, communities rely on unique safety networks, with dispatchers playing a vital role in processing and responding to incidents. Although dispatchers are involved in every interaction, their contributions go underrepresented. This study analyzes text-based incident reports between users and dispatchers, revealing the existing power imbalance in current systems. To enhance transparency and fairness, we propose a two-part solution: initially identifying hidden user-dispatcher interactions, and secondly designing a framework to assign tasks fairly.

To analyze the impact of external spin fluctuations on triplet Cooper pairs within a nematic superconductor, we utilize the self-consistent Born approximation and discover a substantial rise in magnetic susceptibility at a low-energy point directly related to the gap frequency. Furthermore, in the limit where the triplet Cooper pairs' orientation is dynamically determined, this magnetic response exhibits a near-frequency-independent pattern. Such a behavior can be observed in experiments as an apparent decrease in the gap magnitude.

We introduce a key challenge in offline non-convex reinforcement learning where an actor develops policies and a critic evaluates them based on historical data, with the actor striving to close the policy-critic gap. Notably, the critic's goal is to accurately forecast the post-implementation outcome of each policy. The actor's efforts are hindered by two major obstacles: (1) outdated actions in the data set appear relevant but lack practical value, distracting from the target outcome; (2) the critic's forecast is compromised by biased estimates of past rewards. Our work develops a flexible, adaptable method to tackle this problem, Minimax Engaged Learning (MEL), which integrates both criticism and actor-critic training. MEL employs a two-staged training process: first, a demonstration critic identifies and ranks representative policies based on past data; next, the actor targets these top-ranked policies while the demonstration critic monitors the policy-critic gap. Additionally, the critic's forecast is refined by leveraging the actor's policy guidance. Through a range of experiments on diverse offline RL tasks, MEL demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods.

This study tracks the shift in complexity of Western popular music from the 1950s to the 2000s, utilizing information-theoretic methods that delve deeper into song structure than previous analyses. Music recordings from significant historical periods--the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s, 1980s, and 2000s--are measured for informational complexity using text-based analysis. The findings show a notable increase in complexity from the 1950s to the 2000s, with clear distinctions between successive decades and notable peaks in the 1960s and 2000s.

We examine a reinforcement process with multiple entries where a player selects a danger item from a set of N items, and upon encountering it, a token is awarded. This award then initiates a novel "token period," during which the player aims to collect a predetermined number of safe items. Upon collecting these safe items, the token is exchanged for a reward in a fixed location, and the process is restarted. This selection of danger items can be approached in two distinct methodologies - the Monte Carlo method or theoretically, utilizing Markov decision processes. Our asymptotic analysis involves both methods and we find that they converge to a singular, time-independent strategy. To prove this, we first establish convergence of the Monte Carlo method by demonstrating the uniform convergence of the estimated value function to the optimal policy's value function. Next, we show the equivalence of the optimal policy from the Markov decision process to the one found through asymptotic analysis of the Monte Carlo method. Finally, we clarify why approaches differing from the optimal strategy are not desirable by showing that they yield negative expected returns.
We demonstrate through a semantical analysis that the notion of harmony in computational luds is a consistent application of the cut rule.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose cluster ranking by utilizing visual aids, which efficiently leverages human feedback, resulting in substantial time savings of up to 10 times compared to traditional methods. Moreover, our approach can also be applied to historical data to refine existing reward functions, leading to notable performance gains in this domain as well.

We show that Smyth spaces are core-compact if and only if they have a strongest element. This result strengthens a previous finding by J. Paseka [1]. Moreover, this enrichment allows us to simplify and extend Paseka's core-compactness criteria for Smyth spaces.

We're investigating the interaction of multiple circular vortex loops in an ideal two-dimensional fluid, starting with a single loop that can change its topology by shrinking or expanding in a way that conserves angular momentum. Our research shows that loop dynamics are controlled by a massless scalar field, with the number of loops possible depending on the value of a quantized charge parameter. The loops interact through a complex process, with local interactions in each loop's vicinity affecting its movement, and this complexity can be explained by a non-linear interaction between the loop and a surrounding scalar field state.

To estimate treatment effects in the presence of high-dimensional confounders, inverse probability weighting faces significant computational hurdles for modeling complex covariates. A two-stage neural network approach has been proposed, involving a first stage for prediction and a second stage for standardizing weighted outcomes, using IPW estimates. This method can handle both continuous and discrete treatment types and has been demonstrated to converge analytically. The method's performance in estimating treatment effects has been evaluated under various scenarios and shown to outperform current state-of-the-art techniques significantly.

The current understanding of the Standard Model, particularly its weak interaction component, will be presented with a focus on the tau lepton, a crucial aspect of which is the tau decay rate. Theoretical predictions for this quantity serve as a reference point to evaluate experimental findings. The goal is to achieve a precise match between theoretical and experimental results for the tau decay rate, a milestone that will likely result in significant constraints on new beyond-the-SM physics theories. The challenge will be discussed in two phases – the ongoing and the future. In the ongoing phase, the focus is on the Lambda_e tau decays research at the KLOE experiment, while the future phase is centered around the tau lepton research at the future tau-charm factory, a proposed facility designed to study tau and charm particles in detail.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in temperature gradients and rotational rates, thereby creating distinctive wave patterns at the free surface of the rotating liquid. These experiments were conducted alongside numerical simulations by five groups from the MetStr\"om collaboration, utilizing different methods and approaches to validate their results. The obtained wave patterns were then analyzed, compared, and documented to establish benchmarks that can be used to evaluate the performance of atmospheric numerical models in the future.

A common technique for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has drawn statistical analysts to it due to its ease of interpretation in terms of return periods, it also presents a challenge for Bayesian inference. This paper introduces an alternative representation of the Poisson process that makes Bayesian modeling feasible and efficient. This approach can be applied to parameter estimation for extreme events and provides a straightforward method for assessing the similarity of two sets of extreme data. The proposed method is then used to study extreme events such as earthquakes and floods.

In the context of offline reinforcement learning, we address the challenge of maximally exploiting perfectly clean data and mitigating the influence of corrupt samples. By combining existing concepts from reinforcement learning and statistical integrity, we develop a novel method to estimate the Q-function while effectively dismissing corrupt data samples. We also establish a corruption-resilient offline policy learning approach and prove its optimal outcome relative to the conventional offline Q-learning method. We experimentally verify the efficacy of our approach on a range of environments, including basic grid-world and more complex Robinson Crusoe scenarios, and observe that in many instances it yields comparable results to those achieved with perfect data.

This study demonstrates a straightforward proof of the logarithmic concavity of the transition cost associated with a controlled 1-D heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions. This implies the existence and uniqueness of the optimal solution, which we also establish as a variational solution, thereby extending a prior result from J. Y. Yin [SIAM J. Control Optim., 58(3), 2000, pp. 938-969]. Furthermore, we show that at the optimal time for the given initial and final states, the heat source required for transition is represented by a delta function located at the boundary, effectively making the optimal control an impulsive controllability, which we also extend to multi-dimensional cases with similar results.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We addressed two unresolved questions in this research: Firstly, we investigated whether there are distinct categories of out-of-distribution examples by analyzing their distribution patterns across various languages and data sources. Secondly, we determined whether these categories can be identified using existing methods. Our findings revealed that the likelihood of out-of-distribution examples below a model's confidence threshold varies significantly between intervals of 0 to 80% similarity with the training dataset. Additionally, we stratified the out-of-distribution data into three distinct groups and developed novel metrics that achieved superior cross-lingual adaptation and performance comparisons with the current state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines models of self-propelled molecular transport based on nanoscale charge tunneling. We're investigating how these mechanisms, known as Brownian molecular engines, can generate force and move particles by harnessing the fluctuations in electric current from quantum systems. Initially, we explore a simple tunneling circuit and find that it cannot drive the movement of a particle, instead causing it to vibrate randomly. However, we also identify a more complex nanoscale system, represented by the anisotropic tunneling circuit, as a effective driver of particle movement. Through simulation, we predict the characteristics of the system's steady-state movement, and confirm that it matches the behavior of a thermodynamic engine driven by thermal fluctuations. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between the tunneling circuit's design and the force exerted on the particle, revealing a linear connection. Lastly, we explore the possibility of tuning the engine's movement by adjusting the tunneling circuit's properties, and demonstrate how this affects the system's behavior at both hot and cold temperatures.

We analyze an advanced class of transducers called two-way sequential (TS) acceptors, capable of processing infinite word sequences. By establishing a link between acceptance in these systems and finite automata equipped with additional capabilities, we demonstrate that acceptance by a TS acceptor can be broken down into two separate factors: (1) the structure of its initial states and (2) the flow of work it performs over time. This reveals a fine-grained understanding of the computational complexity of these systems and sets the stage for future exploration of one-directional versions of these acceptors, which remain poorly understood. To this end, we introduce a new class of one-directional TS acceptors known as one-way sequential (WS) acceptors and show that acceptance in these systems depends solely on the flow of work they perform, leading to a related but distinct computational complexity class. Consequently, we propose a corresponding hierarchy of acceptance classes tied to the level of work performed in acceptance processes.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 sparked controversy over its parent star, with the APOLLO code now providing insight into the underlying conditions of its formation. By utilizing this code in 2020, researchers found that the most probable mass of GJ 229B lies between 26.3 and 64.8 times the mass of Jupiter, with the code also indicating that this object likely has a mass between 40 and 50 times that of Jupiter. Additionally, the code confirmed that the second most massive brown dwarf, Siar 103, was actually the least probable outcome of its formation, further supporting previous findings based on the calculation of the equation of state of T-dwarfs.

To address the long-standing issue of potential exotic states, specifically focusing on $0^{--}$, this work takes a different approach by introducing a new set of observables to aid in differentiating exotic from conventional state properties. Building upon existing research by R. L. Shuryak et al., this work incorporates perturbative QCD (pQCD) calculations and targets the $\chi(c0)(3870)$ as a $0^{++}$ ground state candidate to calculate $0^{--}$ meson masses. By applying pQCD rules to calculate transition form factors, this work computes the ${\bf J}/\psi$ decay branchings of the $0^{--}$ states, ultimately estimating their exotic and conventional components. Moreover, this work proposes accessing the $0^{--}$ states through the ${\bf J}/\psi$ decays of the tensor mesons $K_2^*(1680)$, $K_2*(1780)$, $K_2*(2025)$, and $f_2(1270)$. If produced in sufficient quantities, the $0^{--}$ states could serve as intermediate states in the study of exotic tetraquark properties, specifically through the $\chi(c0)(3870) \to D^* \bar{D}^-$ decays.

This letter presents preliminary findings on $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ from a combination of data collected by the LHCb experiment between 2010 and 2012, totaling 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data at 7 TeV. The $\phi_s$ value was determined and the results for $\Delta\Gamma_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_d$ were constrained, ultimately leading to the establishment of a constraint on the CKM unitarity triangle relation and providing insight into New Physics influencing the $b\rightarrow s$ transition.

Airborne pathogens can spread through droplets released into the air via speaking, coughing, or breathing. Understanding the mixing of these droplets in a given environment is crucial to forecasting transmission risk. A new study examines this challenge in an urban bus setting, employing numerical simulations of a three-dimensional domain. To characterize mixing, researchers utilized well-mixed and non-uniform frameworks. The latter accounted for turbulence by dividing the bus into discrete sections based on airflow patterns. Another approach considered the bus in a perfect mix environment. For extreme ventilation scenarios, both methods showed comparable results, but significant differences emerged in low ventilation conditions, with the non-uniform framework revealing a clear split of the bus into front, middle, and rear sections. These findings imply a crucial role of ventilation in containing infection spread.

This research focuses on the $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy of $^{137}$Te. Recent studies at IGISOL have revealed the $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectrum of $^{137}$Te. The shell-model calculations were performed to determine the $\beta$-decay rates and the $^{136}$I eigenstates, which were then used to establish a connection with the experimental findings. The theoretical results showed a strong correlation with the observed data. The calculated $\beta$-decay probabilities of $^{135,137}$Te are presented in terms of the log$ft$ values. The influence of the nuclear force components on the $\beta$-decay rates was also investigated through various tidal force parameter variations. The study found that the $\beta$-decay rates of $^{135,137}$Te are highly sensitive to the interactions within the Te and I nuclei.

Double-sided auctions are versatile and have been applied in various fields. 
Their potential benefits to auction participants can, however, be hindered by 
unfair outcomes and lack of guaranteed allocations, which can stem from a lack 
of clear price guidelines. Furthermore, the inherent complexity of double-sided 
auctions makes it challenging for bidders to formulate optimal bidding strategies, 
especially in the face of uncertainty. This paper addresses these issues by 
introducing a validated double-sided auction method that ensures fair prices, 
guaranteed participation, and transparent bidding strategies. We also examine 
the computational efficiency of this approach and provide an illustrative example 
drawn from an actual financial market scenario.

We utilize heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $D_0^*$ and $D_1^*$ mesons, specifically focusing on their respective mass differences and decay constants. By incorporating both perturbative and non-perturbative components into our analysis, we are able to derive theoretical values that align closely with experimental findings. Notably, our results for the $D_0^*-D_0$ mass difference support the standard model's prediction that the $CPT$-violating effect is less than $10^{-15}$ GeV$^2$.

We derive a novel parametric decomposition of directed graphs into periods, which yields valuable insights for analyzing the properties of nonexpansive paths. Our work is particularly significant because it offers a precise characterization of the convex hull of nonexpansive distances between any two vertices of a directed graph. Furthermore, our period decomposition has far-reaching implications for approximating single-sourcing minimum spanning tree and related problems.

We introduce the LANDO method, a kernel-based approach that facilitates the discovery of a optimal linear filter for the dynamic mode decomposition technique without the need to presume a specific linear or nonlinear system model. Our approach adopts a data-driven skepticism stance, skeptical of the underlying system assumptions found in traditional model-based formulations. LANDO employs kernel methods to develop a optimal linear filter for predicting future measurements, and this filter is learned from the data itself through the solution of a non-convex optimization problem. Our method generalizes the previous work on kernel-based dynamic mode decomposition, providing a more accurate and practical approach for solving the prediction problem. Additionally, we show that our method can be applied to both linear and nonlinear system models, but such optimizations result in sub-optimal solutions. Our method's effectiveness is validated through a variety of numerical simulations.

By integrating chess data from Online Chess Repository and chess strategy forums, we analyzed the intricacy and connection of chess openings. Firstly, the chess community data allowed us to identify the most popular openings, their success rates, and the degree of their connection. Additionally, the complex structure of chess openings was revealed through the creation of a chess strategy network, where openings were linked based on shared moves. This investigation also compared the similarity of chess openings using both a traditional method and a novel approach based on random matrix theory, seeking to identify closely related openings. Finally, the analysis of chess openings in relation to professional chess players' skills showed that more intricate openings were associated with advanced players, providing insights into the connection between chess strategies and player expertise.

This research explores the potential for advanced neutron stars, specifically millisecond pulsars, to be created when a white dwarf star consumes another dwarf, resulting in an isolated neutron star remnant. We investigated several evolutionary pathways that could lead to this outcome by analyzing simulations of binary star systems and discovering that in most cases, the white dwarf's ingestion of the secondary star causes it to destabilize and then stabilize again through the absorption of surrounding material. We found that in scenarios where the secondary star is massive enough (>0.15 solar masses), the white dwarf typically undergoes significant instability, spanning millions of years, and ultimately loses approximately 65% of its initial mass. We also identified an interesting relationship, specifically that the mass of the neutron star remnant is directly related to the lower mass boundary of the white dwarf's envelope, which in turn is linked to the initial binary separation of the systems. This relationship, specifically that the mass of the neutron star remnant increases by ~0.05 solar masses for every doubling of the binary separation, holds true across various binary star systems and their respective millisecond pulsar productions. Additionally, we observed that the spin periods of these neutron stars are primarily influenced by the initial mass of the neutron star, with values ranging from tens of milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds. Notably, we found that the spin periods of the neutron star remnant tend to increase slightly in scenarios where the secondary star is less massive, whereas those with more massive secondary stars tend to exhibit little to

This study offers a general theory of nonlocal quantities of motion for Lagrangian Dynamics of any order. We initiated this theoretical framework with Noether's second theorem, where we established nonlocal invariance criteria within the context of Lagrangian Dynamics of any order. We subsequently explored the connection between nonlocal invariance and nonlocal quantities of motion, before establishing a direct relationship between these concepts. We then analyzed the specific case of Lagrangian Dynamics of any order based on a polynomial Lagrangian, where we derived the complete set of Euler equations, along with corresponding nonlocal quantities of motion. Our theoretical framework was further validated by examining a simple model consisting of a particle in a potential, where we calculated the corresponding nonlocal quantities of motion.

This study innovatively combines freehand 3D modeling with shape retrieval tasks by introducing an innovative retrieval approach, dubbed "3D sketch retrieval via 3D drawing". In this context, virtual reality tools enable users to create three-dimensional shapes through natural hand movements, which are then used to search for existing 3D models. By training a deep learning-based classifier to identify the similarity between these virtual hand-drawn shapes and actual 3D model views, we've achieved significant retrieval precision rates of up to 44% and mean average precision rates of up to 36.25% when evaluated using early retrieval metrics. Our research showcases the efficacy of VR-drawing tools in facilitating 3D model searches and highlights their potential to enhance traditional design workflows. From a technical perspective, this research synthesizes three complex areas: volumetric 3D sketching, shape retrieval, and deep learning-based classification, which requires considering multiple optimizations to achieve high performance. Additionally, to our knowledge, this study marks the first attempt to apply VR-drawing to 3D shape retrieval, thus opening up new avenues for research and potential applications.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a daily transformation from scorching hot to relatively cool and vice versa due to its highly eccentric orbit. In 2020, observations by the James Webb Space Telescope were scheduled to take advantage of a special alignment when the planet transits its host star, allowing for detailed analysis of the planet's atmosphere. However, the planned mission was cancelled due to the pandemic, presumably because the coordinates of the planet and the host star had changed. In our study, we updated the coordinates for the planet and the host star using a machine learning tool that analyzes transit observations from a network of telescopes. The network consists of 13 different projects including the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment and the K2 mission, which provided us with accurate data to predict the changed positions of the planet and the host star. The results of these predictions align with previous studies and also match the predictions from another study that used microlensing data.

We examine how a linear relationship between pressure and density affects the outcome of isentropic collapse in a perfect fluid. Through mathematical analysis, we identify two types of potentials that support black hole solutions and speculate on their ability to form such solutions. We also consider the conditions necessary for these potentials to have a physically meaningful origin and discuss the implications for their corresponding scalar field models. Additionally, we investigate the feasibility of forming black hole solutions in the space of generalized Polytropes and Polytropic potentials, highlighting their potential to explain the mass gap phenomenon.

We use the Iyer-Wald formalism to determine how specific parameters affect the emission of gravitational waves by extreme black holes. By incorporating variations in the wave function itself and considering emissions at all levels of non-linearities, we establish a comprehensive framework for studying wave corrections. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that higher non-linearities result in energy loss and particle formation beyond what's predicted by classical theories.

Research has demonstrated that active movement plays a crucial role in recovery after stroke, but specific factors contributing to the benefits of active movement are not yet fully understood. Our study aimed to examine how active limb movement is guided in healthy subjects and individuals who have experienced a stroke. We focused on the effects of three distinct forms of guidance – elastic resistance, position, and velocity constraints – on subject behavior. Subjects were required to complete tasks in a virtual 2D environment using a robotic arm attached to their wrist. Results indicated that when subjected to elastic resistance, subjects' movements were driven by an interaction between their intentions to move and the resistance offered. In contrast, when movements were restricted by position or velocity limits, subjects' interactions with the constraints led to highly variable reactions, including increased movement variability and altered movement timing. These findings suggest that only elastic resistance facilitates effective movement similar to that observed in voluntary movement without constraints. They also imply that robotic therapy incorporating elastic resistance may be beneficial in promoting motor learning and recovery following a stroke.

The dynamic characteristics of Poincaré symmetry and de Sitter gravity are comparable to those of a rotating heat source. By employing the method of soliton gases, we obtain thermodynamic descriptions for both theories. Furthermore, using this framework, we explore the possibility of mapping Poincaré gravity to a system of classical particles interacting via a long-range force. Additionally, we examine the possibility of mapping de Sitter gravity to a system of classical particles interacting via a confining potential. We find that for Poincaré gravity, the mapping is applicable across all stages, whereas for de Sitter gravity, the mapping is applicable beyond the black hole stage. We present a general approach for deriving the dynamic characteristics of any group manifold using the soliton gas method.

Designing parameterized algorithms for specific problems has become a significant area of study within graph theory and combinatorial algorithms. Certain problems, however, can be more effectively tackled through the development of new, parameterized tractability techniques. This study focuses on parameterized algorithms for solving the Upward Planarity problem, particularly in scenarios where the treewidth of a given graph is relatively small. We introduce two such algorithms, one which has a parameterized runtime of $O(3.1719^{\textrm{tw}} t_{\textrm{w}})$ and another with a parameterized runtime of $O(2.21^{\textrm{tw}} t_{\textrm{w}} t_{\textrm{w}}+1)$, both of which significantly improve previous results in the field.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track environmental context and maintain navigation course.
However, these approaches can result in agents making unnecessary detours by storing all encountered objects in memory.
In contrast, our proposed MemoNav agent decides which objects to remember based on its navigation progress, using a simple yet effective policy that favors relevant environmental context over sheer quantity of stored items.
As a result, MemoNav achieves better performance and reduced navigation time compared to existing methods, with results showing its effectiveness in various scenarios.

This paper provides an in-depth analysis of small cells, covering their development, existing implementations, and planned features for future networks. Starting with an overview of LTE-based small cell technologies and associated challenges, the text delves into 5G PC5 communication and near millimeter wave spectrum support. It also explores future enhancements, including massive MIMO, millimeter wave, terahertz communications, and LEO satellite integration, before moving on to discuss quantum communications and metaverse applications. The paper is a revised and expanded version of an initial paper, incorporating feedback from the IEEE TKNE review committee.

Dynamical systems on networks are entwined with the structure of the underlying graph, where local interactions determine global behaviors. This synergy is both beneficial and restrictive - understanding dynamical systems illuminates network dynamics, while fully capturing global effects from local connections poses theoretical and practical limitations. This report outlines key concepts in dynamical systems theory, specifically focusing on linear systems and their spectral characteristics, to facilitate understanding of theoretical frameworks. It also includes representative models from the mathematical literature to highlight diverse approaches to analysis. Finally, it highlights the diverse range of applications in the social sciences and physics.

Building on the operator algebra approach to quantum field theory, we investigate the connection between operator growth and asymptotic behavior in interacting scalar fields. We derive system-specific formulas for the leading and subleading operator growth rates, expressing them through the interaction potential and momentum space coefficients, respectively. These general formulas apply to both weakly coupled scalar theories, such as $\phi^4$, and strongly coupled Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class scalar models. The derived growth rates align with numerical findings in the strongly coupled models, with a detailed explanation provided for the discrepancy in growth rates between weakly and strongly coupled models, especially in the $u\rightarrow0$ limit.

The properties of the Hoyle state, a unique nuclear quantum system, have been studied through an experimental analysis of alpha particle decay from the state at 7.65 MeV in energy, residing in the 0f, 1d, and 1p orbital angular momentum regions. Utilizing the J-PND experiment's data, which included a Tabletop Particle Tracking Chamber for four-dimensional phase-space reconstruction, the angular distributions of alpha particles and their polarization relative to the relative nuclear motion axis were measured. This allowed for characterization of the nuclear transition density between the 23Al ground state and the Hoyle state at 7.65 MeV. Consistent with theoretical calculations based on the no-core shell model, the analysis indicates a significant non-spherical component of the Hoyle state directly decaying into the 23Al ground state, estimated to be approximately 71 percent.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computing dynamic fracture have been achieved for over a decade since research began, and the findings suggest that fracture instability is inevitable and influenced by two inherent scales specific to the material in question. This study uses the phase-field approach and advanced numerical methods to investigate how these scales affect the complexity of fracture instability in two dimensions. The analysis reveals that fracture instability can manifest as oscillatory behavior or tip splitting, with the relative prevalence of each type dependent on the relative standing and moving lengths scales of the material. The research also identifies a critical threshold beyond which instability is prevented, and the findings are supported by a theoretical model that correlates with numerical results. The presence of this threshold and the types of fracture instability it governs can be observed in experiments involving brittle materials, as shown in previous research.

This study explores the capacity of general finite-state channels with feedback, where the transmitting encoder has access to the received information. The research demonstrates that on a finite-field basis, this capacity can be determined by solving a linear programming problem, with constraints related to the channel's feedback connectivity and a specific property concerning the transmission of input sequences. The proof relies on a novel characterization of the channel capacity region, which is achieved by utilizing a specific type of input sequence, known as strong functionals, in conjunction with a construction method that involves the channel's state and auxiliary variables.

A novel class of superfluids known as topological superfluids possesses unique characteristics, supported by both topological invariant quantities and protected by symmetry. We investigate the occurrence of topological superfluidity in a 2D system, specifically the attractive Rashba Hubbard model with spin-orbit coupling. Under conditions of strong Rashba coupling and spin-orbit coupling exceeding a certain threshold, a particular type of topological superfluid is formed, which is comprised of spin-polarized pairs that exhibit both p-wave and spin-singlet properties. This finding is confirmed through numerical simulations employing the Monte Carlo method. Additionally, an important relationship between Rashba and spin-orbit coupling suggests that the latter can be substituted by other factors, including an applied magnetic field. Consequently, a broad range of topological superfluids can potentially be engineered through the incorporation of Rashba coupling and an appropriate choice of external influences.

This study focuses on understanding, interpreting, and addressing the challenges of fact verification and evidence identification within scientific literature, particularly in relation to tabular data. A new dataset, TAB Facts, has been developed to support this endeavor, comprising 2,046 documents and 69,846 facts. Researchers submitted 15 submissions to SemEval-2021 Task 9 (SEM-TAB-FACTS), which aimed to evaluate current table fact verification and evidence-finding tools. A human evaluation revealed that only 2 submissions surpassed a basic threshold of 50% accuracy across all tasks; a subsequent analysis revealed that a table structure prediction model played a key role in enhancing submission quality.

The traditional interpretation of complex numbers in quantum mechanics is examined in light of their application within Schrödinger's equation. It is contended that complex numbers are employed in quantum mechanics as a complex base system rather than simply being a complicated set of real numbers. Evidence from quantum computing has revealed that quantum mechanics can function with real coefficients, yet utilizing complex numbers remains the standard approach in quantum mechanics for solving Schrödinger's equation and understanding quantum phenomena. Two possible reasons for this preference are explored. Firstly, the use of complex numbers facilitates the convergence of wave functions through rapid phase convergence, even with large phase discrepancies. Secondly, even with real coefficients, the complex nature of the wave function enables the tracking of phase and magnitude variations between successive measurements. These properties are demonstrated using a simplified model of a quantum system comprising two states and further exemplified in a 39-dimensional system resembling a quantum oscillator.

This research introduces a modified metric dimension concept suitable for finite graphs, addressing a limitation of the original approach by Dvořák and Vochyanínová. The proposed metric dimension variant optimizes the original method's scalability for finite graphs, yielding a more practical solution. The study also investigates key properties of this trimmed metric dimension, comparing its attributes to those of the original dimension concept.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater flow and water table dynamics. They draw upon Darcy's Law to describe flow velocity, sum the flows from multiple aquifers, apply conservation principles to develop the mass balance equation, and employ numerical methods to resolve issues related to spatial and temporal discretization. 

In the course of my research, I have found that existing resources either fail to provide a step-by-step logical progression or assume a level of advanced knowledge that is not present in the given literature. As such, these notes aim to provide a clear and detailed explanation of the equations, suitable for integration into a textbook or instructional material. 

Furthermore, the section on van Genuchten's approach includes a previously unpublished simplification that resolves issues related to parameter scaling and the curvature of energy function curves. 

Throughout the review, I have sought to adhere strictly to the principles of ground water flow and avoid mixing theoretical and practical content, except in cases where direct relevance is ensured. 

The included mathematical derivations are correct and thoroughly documented, with a focus on explaining complex concepts in a step-by-step manner to facilitate clear understanding.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating sulfur dioxide SO2 through the formation of sulfuric acid. A numerical model was developed to examine various configurations of O3 and UV. Under optimal conditions, using 30 ug/L O3 and 1600 μW/cm² UV, SO2 removal reached levels above 99.9%. A novel reactor design involving baffle inserts has been proposed to enhance mass transfer between O3 and SO2, resulting in a significant boost in destruction efficiency to 98.5% while reducing energy consumption by 64%. Furthermore, simulations showed that low O3 consumption could be achieved by increasing UV intensity. These findings suggest that integrating UV and O3 has great potential to become a highly effective and energy-efficient method for SO2 removal in flue gas.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in testing and validating their designs. To address this issue, we have developed a modular, open-source simulation environment utilizing SystemC, compatible with Synopsys VCD files. This framework includes a range of reusable components to swiftly create and execute virtual platforms for neuromorphic designs in multi-core systems. Furthermore, we have devised a novel event-driven simulation method to enhance performance, resulting in near-native speeds in simulation-driven benchmarks.

Machine learning models known as "decision forests" typically produce certain outcomes, but such models can also generate probabilistic results, as seen in "decision trees of doubt". This research explores a novel approach to creating argument-based decision forests that account for quantities of uncertainty. We develop a decision forest framework called "Indecision Forests (IDFs)", which allows computers to learn from pairs of argumentative statements by identifying uncertain premises that can lead to conflicting conclusions. This framework reveals that, in cases of uncertainty, negation is not necessarily equivalent to contradiction, a finding that has implications for natural language processing. We also demonstrate how IDFs can be applied to reason about concrete events and provide intuition behind their decisions.

The DTW pruning method has gained popularity over recent years due to its capacity to enhance the efficiency of DTW distance computation through effective reduction strategies. One core idea behind pruned DTW is to discard signal segments that won't lead to optimal alignments, thus minimizing unneeded computations. The current version of pruned DTW method only determines whether a discarding operation is permissible after it has been invoked. This paper proposes an enhanced version called Early Discarding PrunedDTW (EDPD) that allows for in-advance assessment of whether a discarding operation can take place. The proposed EDPD method yields better performance than the standard pruned DTW method across various similarity search tasks and settings.

Current educational tools in software testing lack intelligent support, with most relying on pre-recorded videos or expert-created tutorials. To address this gap, a study investigated the effectiveness of two testing education approaches: one that incorporated human-like virtual instructors and another with AI-driven testing tools. The research compared how these tools affected learning outcomes, including conceptual understanding and practical skills, among 120 university students. The results showed that the instructor-based approach yielded better outcomes in terms of conceptual understanding, while the AI-driven method led to superior practical skills. The study's findings have implications for the design of educational tools, with potential applications extending to other technical subjects.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data security. However, existing approaches often fail to provide explanations for certain models, such as deep neural networks, or struggle to generalize such explanations to other datasets. This research develops a novel approach that integrates the strengths of two distinct methods: concept analysis for understanding model decision-making and inductive logic programming for prescribing which data features contribute to model outcomes. This combined method enables the generation of detailed, data-set-agnostic explanations for deep neural networks, thus filling a significant gap in the literature. Examples demonstrating the efficacy of this approach can be found in the supplied supplementary material.

Over-blurring refers to the tendency of machine learning models to lose input details, which is particularly common in graph convolutional networks (GCNs). A new perspective on over-blurring in GCNs is offered from an optimization standpoint. It is demonstrated that feed-forward neural networks face a challenge related to optimal solutions - inputs with high activation values must be paired with large gradient values. This requirement makes it impossible to achieve precise input details without compromising other nodes' information. An algorithm is introduced to simulate over-blurring in specific models, which is then used to investigate the (semi-)supervised over-blurring risk in various scenarios. Notably, the risk becomes more pronounced in settings with limited data. To mitigate over-blurring, a new strategy called Input Focus loss is proposed. Experiments on six benchmark datasets reveal that IF-loss reduces blurring and yields comparable or superior results compared to existing methods.

A search for dark matter and a measurement of its mass are carried out in events with a positively charged lepton (either an electron or a muon), an inherently neutrally charged Z boson, and varying amounts of activity in the proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy level, conducted within the CMS experiment at the LHC, utilizing a dataset with a 35.9 inverse femtobarns exposure. The investigation focuses on either one or two oppositely charged leptons, looking for signs of dark matter produced in association with a Z boson through either a Higgs boson or top quark pair, with the Z boson decaying into two bosons. The investigators look at multiple signal regions, including events above a high threshold of activity in the central mass range of the proton-proton collisions. No significant signs are observed as of the summer 2016 data analysis cutoff. The researchers set a 95% confidence level upper limit on two-parton production of a Z boson and a dark matter particle, with masses up to 12 GeV, as well as on dark matter pairs ranging from 25 to 200 GeV, with cross-sections ranging from a few femtobarns to less than a femtobarn, depending on the mass.

Building upon previous research by Bozek and Straka [1], further insights into relativistic kinetic theory have been gained through the derivation of Liouville density in a $k_\perp$-dependent reference frame. In this framework, a relativistic $f_{1T}$ distribution function, similar to its $1$D counterpart, has been introduced by Bozek and Straka [2]. However, the approach taken here differs from their method of adding a transverse component to the distribution function. Instead, a new Liouville density in a $k_\perp$-dependent framework has been established, and its relationship to the standard Liouville density is demonstrated by applying a Wigner transformation. Furthermore, the approach taken here facilitates the direct identification of a new distribution function, $f_{1T}$. In addition to the derivation of this distribution function, a relativistic $f_{1L}$ distribution function in a $k_\perp$-dependent framework has been introduced by modifying the $f_{1T}$ function.

We define a topological space to be stock-filled if it has a base composed of exhausted collections of open sets, each of which has a finite index. Our research reveals that any such space is homeomorphic to a limit of topological groups when treated as a certain type of categorical product.
