Moreover, the lack of a comprehensive framework has made it challenging for researchers to validate and compare the efficacy of different approaches, limiting their adoption in practical settings, and even led to the development of similar solutions independently, and sometimes differently, by different researchers, and sometimes in a published form. To address these issues, we created LibOPT - an open-source platform for rapid prototyping and efficient implementation of soft optimization techniques, and used it to re-implement existing algorithms creatively, and validate our solutions through thorough analysis, and even discovered that, surprisingly, some re-implemented algorithms performed better than their original versions, and sometimes compared to other similar algorithms, and even discovered that, surprisingly, some re-implemented algorithms performed better than their original versions, and sometimes compared to other similar algorithms.

In this study, we establish a fundamental result that links the transitivity degree of a group action with a characteristic shape parameter, thereby yielding significant conclusions across multiple mathematical domains, including projective geometry, algebraic statistics, and enumeration theory. Our key finding stems from an interpretation of the transitivity degree as an extended version of the degree of a projective bundle, a concept initially explored by Eisenbud, Flatto, and Katz. This connection enables us to draw diverse applications, such as analyzing orbit spaces, enumerating non-equivalent configurations, and studying invariant ring properties.

In this review, we'll examine how the principles of quantum mechanics and general relativity are applied to particles in a spacetime where coordinates do not follow the standard ordering. Our investigation will involve analyzing how key aspects of quantum field theory behave in this non-standard spacetime, with a focus on the functional renormalization group as a versatile tool. We'll also explore the implications of our findings for the identities of elementary particles and the cohesion of spacetime itself.

We introduce an innovative approach called the transient-voltage technique, which employs two-photon absorption to measure local electric current in three-dimensional single-crystalline diamond samples. This method doesn't interfere with charge transport with the use of contactless measurements, enabling comprehensive 3D analysis of the sample's electrical properties. We apply this method to a sample of single-crystalline diamond, known for its semi-insulating properties, to map its charge transport properties. Results show that we can accurately model the sample's electrical behavior under transient conditions, achieving a high degree of precision in local current mapping. This method has broad applications in analyzing the electrical properties of wide bandgap materials.

Social media platforms are facing significant challenges due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny, which are damaging online communities. While numerous studies have focused on detecting toxic content, few have targeted misogyny specifically. Our research contributes to filling this knowledge gap by introducing a novel dataset for misogyny detection and categorization within Arabic social media. We also propose an advanced deep multi-task model, termed iMTELO, which simultaneously tackles classification and generation tasks to enhance overall performance. Our findings indicate that iMTELO surpasses the performance of relevant single-task models, thus establishing a crucial benchmark for future research.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations, which involve an auxiliary condition related to the equation's generator. By applying a comparison theorem, we establish existence and uniqueness for these equations under Lipschitz conditions, both with and without delay, respectively. Furthermore, we explore the key properties of the generated operator and demonstrate its continuity.

We examine how varying environmental characteristics and modeling uncertainty
affect the performance of optimal control methods when applied to dynamic systems.
Initial findings suggest that in the presence of uncertainty, controllers generated
via traditional "open-loop" optimization last only a short time before deteriorating.
Conversely, "closed-loop" methods, which involve using data from the environment to
update policy parameters, perform better in uncertain environments, but struggle
when faced with sudden changes in system behavior.
To improve performance in uncertain settings, we present a novel algorithm that
combines policy search with probabilistic modeling of the system's dynamics.
This approach allows for the development of robust regulators, effective in a range of
scenarios from known parameters to complete ambiguity.

We introduce a unified model for analyzing interference in distributed computation systems with multiple stages. Our framework accommodates various scenarios with arbitrary numbers of nodes, distributed computation schemes, and interference models. A sample distribution computation example illustrates how to model complex systems within our framework, which enables the derivation of fundamental performance metrics and limits. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our framework to the caching problem by providing novel inner and outer bounds for a specific instance with multiple caches and a single server.

We establish a framework for the Scott model of PCF within univalent type theory, demonstrating that its core properties - including stability, continuity, and surjectivity - can be formulated purely dependently on the universal properties of the weakly increasing sequence type and the corresponding continuous functions. This formulation maintains full compatibility with the standard constructive set-theoretic framework.

This study employs the concept of "standard vectors" to analyze the degeneration of Eisenstein Series from the generic to special forms, combining concepts of lattices, orbits, and Schubert varieties to explore this phenomenon within the context of $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

This research focuses on addressing the security risks associated with untrusted wireless communication links used in controlling robots. Theoretical foundations are developed to ensure that robot movements from a secure initial state remain secure despite experiencing malicious data transmissions. The concept of Control Barrier Functions is adapted to create a Security Barrier Function, which serves as the key component in designing secure control strategies. Specifically, a high-level Strategy Function is proposed to determine the optimal wireless data transmission policy given a robot's secure state trajectory. Conversely, a low-level Security Buffer Function is identified to maintain secure movements even in the presence of malicious data. A hybrid system approach is employed to combine these functions and establish a Security-in-Verification (SIV) framework. Finally, security verification and synthesis are realized through optimization techniques and case studies involving a mobile robotic arm are conducted to demonstrate our approach.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to derive computational representations and functionality from naturally occurring texts, encompassing speech and writing. Text summarization, a significant aspect of natural language processing, aims to compress lengthy documents into manageable sizes while retaining crucial information. This review presents an overview of text summarization techniques and proposes a graph-based approach for extractive summarization, highlighting the benefits of incorporating sentence similarity graphs and scoring functions to facilitate informed summary selection.

Researchers have successfully implemented the quantum hydrodynamics approach to study weakly interacting Bose-Einstein condensates. This involves deriving a set of nonlinear hydrodynamic equations that capture the quantum nature of the condensate. However, the process of operator discretization is a critical step that can affect the accuracy and long-term stability of the numerical solution. A novel method has been introduced to determine the optimal parameters for discretizing the operator in a way that minimizes errors and maintains a high level of precision. This technique has been successfully tested in a Bose-Einstein condensate with a rotating core and has shown significant improvements over existing methods.

This study explores the distinctness of meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, building upon previous work by the second author and D. Dong. Our research extends their findings to cover cases involving non-algebraic varieties of arbitrary dimension.

Polynomial system solving is a fundamental concept with wide-ranging applications to various fields like algebra, geometry, and dynamic systems. The notion of nondegenerate solutions is significant in addressing real solutions, and locating such solutions within a specific real locus becomes a crucial task. We have developed a new signature-based method to determine the dimension and local coordinates of the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system. By utilizing a division lemma, we can derive a set of nondegenerate loci of lower dimensional subsystems, and the associated codimension is calculated through the number of parameters in the signature. We have established the nondegenerate locus as a finite set of points known as numerical codimension instances, and demonstrated its application through a multitude of examples.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we determined that $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess data aligns with a modified Tsai-Huang mass-yield approach. Additionally, we found that the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess direct photon $R_{A|central}}$ values for Cu$+$Cu collisions are lower than those for Au$+$Au collisions, and we observed that the $R_{A|central}}$ values for Cu$+$Cu collisions follow the trend of increasing with decreasing system size compared to $p$+$p$ collisions.

A significant problem in combinatorial design theory, known as Turan's Tetrahedron Problem, seeks to determine the minimum number of edges in a hypergraph that contains no complete tetrahedron. We addressed a modified version of this question by finding the least number of edges in a 3-dimensional hypergraph that contains no complete tetrahedron, and measuring the distance between these edges using the $\ell_2$-norm. Our work built upon previous research by Bollobas, and further refined his general results for the $\ell_1$-norm.

When displaying line segments, particularly on digital maps, aliasing can occur, causing jagged edges that are noticeable at higher zoom levels. This issue is commonly seen in maps and is characterized by jagged ends on map features. Most anti-aliasing techniques are designed to address rendering limitations, but they often fail to address the specific aliasing issues seen on line joins. Existing anti-aliasing methods involve modifying pixel rendering techniques and involve complex calculations, making them difficult to implement in real-time applications. Real-time map rendering requires fast and efficient processing to maintain smooth panning and scrolling performance. This study introduces an effective spatial anti-aliasing rendering method specifically designed for line joins on map features, aiming to improve visual quality while maintaining efficient processing times.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), and numerical tests confirm this convergence rate.

The observed gamma-ray emitting pulsars in the galaxy serve as a reliable indicator of its underlying magnetic field strength and distribution. By assuming that these pulsars emit gamma-rays when their rotational energy exceeds the threshold for radiative ejection, researchers estimate the maximum magnetic field strength within a specific area of the galaxy and find it to be in the range of 10 to 10^9 Gauss. To further study the magnetic field, researchers analyze its correlation with the galaxy's rotation rate, revealing a noticeable discrepancy in the outer regions. By integrating the observed pulsar luminosities and applying the principle of detailed balance, researchers estimate the total power output from these pulsars and find it to be roughly 3.5 x 10^40 erg/s. The combination of these findings and other observations support the conclusion that the galaxy's magnetic field plays a crucial role in powering its high-energy emission.

This research introduces a new multi-class dataset for image classification called WeatherCats, which consists of 15,000 labeled feline image segments, each accompanied by descriptive metadata. The dataset was crowdsourced from two popular image sharing platforms: Flickr and Instagram. The team conducted a thorough examination of convolutional neural networks, building on the success of existing work that classified images into two categories: sunny or cloudy. Evaluations were performed using two distinct metrics: classification accuracy and categorical balance. To mitigate dataset bias and enhance model generalisation, the team employed data augmentation techniques tailored to the specific needs of this dataset. Additionally, a comprehensive set of architectural variations of CNN models was designed to accommodate the varying image sizes encountered in real-world applications. The experiments demonstrated that a optimized CNN model, augmented with data augmentation tactics, could achieve exceptional results, surpassing state-of-the-art performance benchmarks. The proposed method attained an average accuracy of 93.53% across 15 categories, while also achieving a categorical balance score of 0.8975. Notably, the data augmentation tactics contributed approximately 9% to the overall accuracy improvement. The research further highlights that incorporating a dropout layer at 0.25 yielded a 2% improvement in accuracy. The excellence of the results was further validated through the application of statistical tests, including two-tailed t-tests and bootstrap resampling analysis. The research findings and accompanying materials have been made publicly available for the purpose of facilitating future research and advancements in this domain.
The Interactions of Social Standards about Climate Change: Science, Institutions and Economics

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility in handling delicate objects, however their flexibility also makes them more complex to control. To address this issue, we have developed a model-based control approach that leverages the Koopman operator theory to incorporate nonlinear effects, maintaining simplicity in design. The proposed method consists of three key components: online linear model identification, system control, and actuation planning. To facilitate online linear model identification, we have integrated the Koopman operator theory into the dynamic model analysis of nonlinear systems. Furthermore, we have devised a control approach that utilizes the identified linear model, ensuring it remains close to the original nonlinear system. Lastly, we have developed an actuation sequence controller to account for physical limitations and online linear model discrepancies. The efficacy of this framework has been demonstrated through simulations and actual deployments of a soft multi-fingered gripper, handling both a flexible rod and a delicate electronic component successfully.

Inspired by the organic growth in natural evolution, we introduce a generalized gradient descent framework, adaptable to various underlying systems and their corresponding dynamics. This framework is known as Organic Gradient Descent (OGD) and can be reinterpreted as a specialized form of Evolutionary Optimization, maintaining similar performance characteristics to standard gradient descent methods. Notably, OGD offers a more natural and accessible learning experience for humans, making it a suitable choice for a wide range of real-world applications. By applying OGD to artificial neural networks, we observe improved search efficiency and a higher success rate in finding optimal solutions, particularly in tasks involving limited training data and strict performance constraints.

High-energy radiosources are essentially youthful transients. We discovered a brand-new radiosource, J2102+6015, at a distance of approximately 6.8 billion light years. This source exhibits a youthful appearance consistent with other powerful radiosources at the same distance period. We observed that J2102+6015 exhibits an extremely complex morphology with multiple distinct components. We analyzed the source's spectral characteristics and found that its spectral index is negative, suggesting kpc-scale kinked jets or an interaction with the intergalactic medium as potential explanations. Additionally, J2102+6015 exhibits high energy power, indicating an exceptionally short synchrotron cooling time. We speculate that this source is likely in an early arched stage similar to Pictor A, but requires further observation for confirmation.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, specifically those with non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC). Current clinical information, though valuable, is deemed insufficient for precise survival predictions. To overcome this limitation, this study leverages the capabilities of machine learning, combining clinical and genomic data with text information from clinical reports. By incorporating a two-stage classification framework, this model can effectively identify high and low risk patients, outperforming existing single-feature models. To increase accuracy and fairness, this patient risk assessment was re-evaluated using Bayesian analysis. The findings show that incorporating multiple data types significantly enhances machine learning capabilities, while the proposed model surpasses current single-feature models by up to 12%. Furthermore, Bayesian re-assessment boosts patient safety and minimizes bias in predictions.

A burgeoning area of research, combining Natural Language Processing and Reinforcement Learning, focuses on employing natural language to describe states within RL frameworks. Despite significant advancements in NLP and RL, this subspecialty of NLP/RL has received relatively fewer mentions in academic literature so far. We aim to shed light on the current status of NL state description for RL through an overview of its core aspects, starting with an examination of its underlying principles and subsequent surveys of prominent models and evaluation metrics. We also discuss prevailing challenges and prospective future research directions.

A novel approach to derived cosmological data objects is presented, which utilizes machine learning to transfer knowledge from high precision simulations to real-time observations. This method bypasses the requirement for running cosmological simulations with various parameters by leveraging existing simulations and analytical models to train a neural network. The network can then be applied to observe only a handful of spectra to produce a detailed density power spectrum with minimal uncertainty. This technique holds significant potential for enabling accurate measurements of the density power spectrum from upcoming surveys, such as the Legacy Quasar Initiative, which will conduct over 400,000 spectroscopic observations.

The concept of U(∅)-free structures is applicable to any type of algebraic system and is particularly interesting when considered in the context of Lie algebras. By examining U(∅)-free structures of Lie algebras of differential operators, we obtain a categorical duality between certain classes of Lie algebras and polynomial rings. Additionally, we discover that this duality is self-dual, which has significant implications for potential generalizations to other types of Lie algebras.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a uniform set of techniques to assess sentiment from these datasets.
Our proposed model, an LSTM-based framework, incorporates various techniques such as word,
character, and word/character-level n-gram tokenization, along with word/character-level
embedding using both word2vec and textstat, all within the context of an LSTM architecture.
Our research demonstrates that by combining word and character-level tokenization and
embedding methods, along with the selection of suitable parameters, we can achieve high
levels of accuracy in sentiment classification, with results exceeding 98%.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved notable success.
However, developing a scalable chat system poses a significant challenge, mainly
due to the requirement of numerous user interactions to fine-tune it.
Our proposed framework addresses this issue by integrating a pre-defined role to
streamline open-domain chat conversations, allowing the system to generate more
relevant and coherent responses. Furthermore, we optimized the user input
processing to eliminate the need for annotated data, making the system more
efficient. By leveraging large language models and enhancing user input, our
system outperformed comparisons in multiple evaluation metrics.

The 2015 discovery of GW150914 marked a historic moment in science as it represented the first detection of a binary black hole merger through gravitational waves. Following this, researchers found that the gravitational field generated by the event persisted for an extended period, a phenomenon known as the gravitational wave memory. This study explores the likelihood of encountering such memories in future observations. By analyzing data from the LIGO/Virgo observations through four events, researchers found that the chances of encountering a memory-induced disturbance in a day's worth of data is less than a percent. However, although the likelihood is low, the impact could be substantial as it would result in a significant increase in data processing demands.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework proposes that a super-heavy neutrino mass arises from a symmetry-breaking phase transition, which also generates a massive neutrino cosmologically and produces stochastic gravitational waves detectable by next-generation instruments. This scenario can be realized within the framework of peV-scale leptogenesis, which predicts the existence of additional Higgs bosons heavy enough to be detected via direct search and collider experiments. Additionally, this scenario implies the creation of super-heavy SUSY particles, which might be produced in particle collider experiments or observed in searches for high-energy cosmic rays containing SUSY particles.

A fundamental query understanding capability can be developed by integrating causal reasoning and subtle hint detection abilities into a single framework. A symbol-based representation for implicit cues, which incorporates the concept of 'pointing' as a form of communication, allows for the interpretation of cues through a signaling game framework. This approach enables a to-date unseen level of implicit cue interpretation, as demonstrated by experimental results showing a significant reduction in errors on complex causal graph challenges.

To enhance semantic technology and address the issue of limited semantic coverage, expanding vocabulary with new terms is crucial. One approach to this involves learning new terms based on existing context and semantically related words. However, existing methods face several limitations; for example, they often rely on supervised learning, are data-hungry, or only effective in specific domains. A new hybrid approach is proposed to overcome these limitations by integrating Naive Bayes classification with latent semantic theory. This model leverages contextual information from existing terms to inform new term predictions, utilizing document collection statistics similar to latent semantic indexing. By training the model using existing terms and reinforcing its latent structure, new terms can be predicted based on their context similarity to existing terms. This model represents a significant step towards semi-supervised learning and is a valuable addition to semantic technology, particularly in domains where large-scale corpora are available.

Users interacting with products in online sessions exhibits a diverse range of behaviors, from casually browsing to intensely purchasing. Current recommendation systems fall short in addressing the distinct needs across these various session types. To alleviate this limitation, our proposed session-based recommendation framework leverages the session data to generate actionable recommendations tailored to users' actions within a given online environment. Specifically, our framework employs a candidate rank model that re-ranks candidate items by their relevance to the user's current path, thereby outperforming state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins, as evidenced by superior results in A/B testing and significant increases in sales and revenue.

We examine the behavior of colloidal dimers as they navigate through a fluid with increasing entropy, using Brownian dynamics simulations. The strength of the dimer bond is evaluated based on the frequency of bond formation and breakage, and this analysis shows that the colloid's size and the distance between its components significantly impact the bond strength. Additionally, we discover that the movement of the colloid's tail affects the bond strength, and this occurrence is attributed to the tail's mechanical interaction with the surrounding fluid. This study is followed by an in-depth discussion of the dynamic behavior of the colloid dimers and their similarities with single colloids in activity gradients.

A comprehensive approach is proposed to tackle single-phase flow and transport in a three-dimensional discrete fracture framework. This method employs a novel mesh coupling technique that merges two different domains: a fractured domain modeled using a conforming multi-dimensional mesh. To achieve high precision, specialized numerical operators are developed for fluid flow and transport in the fractured domain. Furthermore, an accurate implementation of fluid flow and transport is achieved across the fracture-matrix interface through a designated interface domain. This approach is put to the test on various complex fracture-matrix models, showcasing notable convergence in simulations. Additionally, comparisons with alternative methods, such as the AFD method, reveal notable results.

This study proposes an innovative technique for maintaining structured patterns in swarms of autonomous vehicles. Our method draws from point set registration in computer science. We have developed a novel, centroid-based approach for autonomous vehicles. Our algorithm calculates the centroid of the swarm's patterned flight path and estimates the lead vehicle's position through distance calculation. Each vehicle then adjusts its speed to converge towards the centroid, with surrounding vehicles modulating their pace to avoid collisions. To test our method's efficacy, we simulated a collision avoidance scenario within a point cloud environment and demonstrated its application in maintaining square and triangular patterns.

This research delves into the properties of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that its eigenvalues are real and that at least one eigenvalue equals 1. Furthermore, we establish the criteria under which the Seidel matrix's characteristic polynomial has a root of 1, and we investigate the Seidel matrix's range and its relationship with the graph's diameter and the minimum spectral radius of the graph's bipartite double.

We're investigating a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations with delays within the context of a fractional Brownian motion. These types of delay equations are subject to fractional stochastic stability, which is not covered by traditional stochastic tools. Our approach involves applying Verceles-Duncan-Iscoe type arguments and incorporating mean-field interactions, leading to a first-order necessary condition for optimality. Utilizing the fractional Brownian motion's properties, we've established a key estimate that enables us to bypass issues related to delay functions' properties and verify the existence of a solution. Additionally, we've provided an illustrative example involving a log-type utility function.

We're investigating the unique finite-band elliptic operators of the Dirac type within the context of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$. These operators can be represented as a sum of a self-adjoint part and a non-self-adjoint part. Given that the non-self-adjoint component is relatively compact, we develop a method to compute the $m$-th eigenvalue of the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator for any positive or negative value of $m$. These eigenvalues are expressed as a function of two variables, $t$ and $s$, where $t$ represents the magnitude of $m$, and $s$ indicates the sign of $m$, resulting in a two-variable function, $\Gamma(t,s)$. Additionally, we establish a model that demonstrates periodic behavior in the real number plane and analyze the local minima and maxima of this function to gain further insight into its periodic nature.

This research introduces an analytical framework for a two-tier vehicular network. This framework incorporates mobile vehicle relays within a larger network supported by roadside units. The primary focus of this model lies in its application to low-speed vehicular networks. The analytical method employs a stochastic approach based on the union-bound principle and a determined interference threshold. The model's performance is assessed using a determined metric, which is then used to derive a bounding probability expression for link reliability. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through a case study, which showcases its ability to account for diverse parameters such as vehicle speeds, channel conditions, and the placement of relays and roadside units.

Wikipedia's potential for addressing societal issues lies in its vast, extensively researched knowledge base. However, the site's openness to editing poses a risk, as malicious actors could compromise its credibility by intentionally spreading false information. To combat this concern, Wikipedia employs a system that flags and labels potentially contentious content - labeled articles often undergo revision to ensure their validity. Our research seeks to identify unproblematic content that tends to become contentious over time, with the aim of preventing potential issues. By analyzing editing patterns and correlation metrics, we developed a machine-learning model that can predict and mark articles at risk of becoming contentious with high accuracy, at a computational cost comparable to the existing Wikipedia system.

Machine learning systems face significant challenges when adapting to scenarios that require relying on external experts due to privacy and confidentiality concerns. In such situations, decision-makers may only share the outcomes of their choices, rather than the underlying reasoning processes. This limitation hinders the development of transfer learning methods, which struggle to effectively utilize this limited information. To address this issue, a new approach, known as Decision-Based Black-Box Knowledge Transfer, is proposed to bridge the gap between hidden decision-making processes and publicly accessible outcomes. By leveraging this information, a life-critical system known as the Autonomic Decision System is developed, which can facilitate zero-shot knowledge transfer in high-stakes domains.

Researchers have explored the decays $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$, $\bar{B}^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$, and $\bar{B}^0_s\to D^0 \bar{K}^0 K^0_S$ using a dataset consisting of 3 ab^{-1} of integrated luminosity collected by the LHCb detector during 7 TeV and 8 TeV proton-proton collisions. For the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay, they derived a branching fraction of (3.12 +/- 0.29 (stat) +/- 0.14 (syst)) * 10^{-4}, which aligns with theoretical predictions based on perturbative QCD. Furthermore, the study represents the first observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay with a corresponding branching fraction of (2.88 +/- 0.37 (stat) +/- 0.18 (syst)) * 10^{-4}.

We've developed a proof that shows T-duality can be applied to a wide variety of twisted circle configurations, and the resulting topological T-duality transformation can be clearly described through a graphical representation. By incorporating Brownian motions and twistings, our model encompasses a range of complex systems, including those with magnetic charges and non-trivial B-fields. The topological T-duality framework can be seen as a type of gauge transformation that effectively eliminates charges, and it provides a unified system for describing various electrical configurations. The key properties of our model can be deduced from basic principles and relate to deep connections in string theory, making them fundamental to the study of the moduli space of string vacua.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, acquiring expert demonstrations on complex tasks is often costly, making the imitation learning approach less practical in real-world scenarios. To overcome this challenge, we propose co-imitation training, a novel technique that learns both expert and student policies simultaneously. By doing so, the student can benefit from seeing the expert's actions without incurring the cost of data collection, and the expert's policy is refined through interaction with the student. In addition, we address the issue of data imbalance between expert and student actions, and evaluate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to tasks involving mixed observation spaces in both continuous and discrete action settings.

This study proposes a metric function that yields an optimal error-correction performance for pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) channel coding. The calculated code performance matches the theoretical values obtained from the union bound under a general assumption. The paper also presents a novel method for determining the bit error ratio (BER) and the bit/phase error ratio (BER/PME) within a specific error range, which significantly reduces simulation complexity and increases accuracy compared to existing methods that use the Berupper function.

A complex and versatile communication tool, the human hand enables individuals to engage in a diverse range of activities from delicate manipulations to dynamic gestures, interacting with various objects in a multitude of settings and environments. This extensive functionality poses significant challenges to hand gesture tracking and accurate 3D reconstruction, particularly when operating outside controlled conditions. To address these challenges, we have developed a novel and universal approach that tracks individual hands in a sequence of depth point cloud frames, simultaneously classifying the user's interactions with visible objects. Our method utilizes a depth-based 3D skeleton hand model, operating directly on raw depth videos without requiring 2D keypoint tracking, thereby enhancing precision and robustness. By applying a sophisticated object-based representation, we are able to accurately model the interactions, reconstructing objects and tracking their movements despite occlusions. Extensive testing on a large real-world dataset confirms the superior performance of our method, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance on established hand tracking and gesture recognition benchmarks, while consistently demonstrating improved tracking and reconstruction stability. Notably, our approach demonstrates exceptional performance even in an evaluation without any pre-training or data augmentation, highlighting its versatility and general applicability.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a 4-letter alphabet and interleaving number 2, based on a suitable presentation. Using this reduced model, we establish the charts for generators' orbits and develop a algorithmic method to construct the group table, which we also outline.

A novel markerless system has been developed, capable of adjusting a depth sensor's field of view to optimize processing performance without the need for additional hardware or setup instructions. Additionally, the system can accurately calculate the position and orientation of the end-effector from the depth sensor's data. A machine learning-based approach, specifically transfer learning using pre-trained models, has been effective in achieving precise results within a short time frame. The proposed system demonstrates effective real-time performance, with adjustable settings allowing for optimal results to be achieved within a confined time frame.

A new interference model has been introduced, which posits that interference occurs when the k nearest neighbors of a subject are treated. Building on this framework, an adaptive method is developed to identify therapy interference in randomized controlled trials with continuous outcomes. The proposed approach leverages a nonparametric estimator of the conditional mean, enhances it with a sensitivity analysis to account for treatment effects and establishes confidence intervals for the treatment effect under the k-neighbor interference model. Crucially, it enables the determination of the minimum value of k for which the treatment effect becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero. Notably, within this framework, there isn't a single 'correct' value of k; rather, its choice depends on the researcher's willingness to tolerate treatment interference. The methodology is demonstrated through simulations and validated using data from two actual trials.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a neutron star are re-examined, specifically focusing on how a particular mediation process affects these emissions. The analysis shows that this mediation process can lead to a significant increase, up to six orders of magnitude, in neutrino emissions compared to previous estimates. The likelihood of detecting these signals with future neutrino detectors is also considered.

Introducing ShapePipe, a groundbreaking, open-source automated pipeline designed for precise galaxy shape measurement, specifically optimized for use with deep optical surveys. By integrating the angular meta-data analysis technique from the Ngmix software with the Galfit profiler, ShapePipe delivers accurate results even for intricate galaxies, even when they heavily distorted. To validate the pipeline's accuracy, a comprehensive comparison was conducted with the ngmix pipeline on a substantial dataset consisting of 896,472 galaxies from the UNIONS/CFIS project after combining three distinct quarts. By employing ShapePipe on this dataset, a comprehensive weak-lensing map was generated that spans an area of approximately 402 square degrees with the highest precision achieved so far in the red wavelength range.

A distinctive case of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem yields the convergence of points in $\Gamma$ modulo $\Lambda$ along with their translates by elements of $\Gamma$, as the size of the involved squares and triangles grows infinitely large, across all flat, two-dimensional shapes $\Gamma$ and $\Lambda$. The underlying proof relies on certain properties of quasi-periodic functions originating from the construction of Hecke algebra, a field of study critical to number theory. The findings build upon a 1924 notion introduced by Hecke, suggesting the emergence of a specific type of quasi-periodic function as the dominant component in the general, projective $L^2$ space associated with a surface $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$.

The present research extends the traditional Kronecker-Weyl outcome by showing that, given any two real, linearly independent numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the sequence of points $(\alpha x + \beta y)_{x,y=1,2,\ldots}$ becomes evenly distributed across the boundary of the unit circle in a specific sense, as their values $x$ and $y$ become infinitely large. Additionally, a related diophantine approximation outcome is established, indicating that, given almost all real, linearly independent numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the sequence of best approximating rational numbers $(p/q)_{p,q=1,2,\ldots}$, as the denominators $p$ and $

We prove that for k-rational singularities on local complete pairs (X, x), the category of k-rational singularities is equivalent to the category of k-Du Bois singularities, which is also equivalent to the category of FSN singularities. Additionally, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for local complete pairs (X, x) to be k-rational or k-Du Bois, and use these conditions to characterize k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities in terms of an analytic category.

We've discovered a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition in the lattice Heisenberg spin system \ CeRhAl, which is caused by the directional influence on the nearest-neighbor exchange interactions. The BKT transition temperature in this system is relatively high and is close to 17 Kelvin, which is also the temperature at which it changes from antiferromagnetic to paramagnetic. Using nuclear magnetic resonance, we were able to measure the magnetic properties on small samples under directional exchange variations, and these results confirm that the BKT transition occurs. Due to the small size of our samples, we were limited to a magnetic field of one Tesla, which is too small to study the BKT transition in detail. Nevertheless, our results provide a foundation for further research on directional exchange in Heisenberg spin systems.

We propose a theoretical framework called "Shadow Matter" to describe sterile neutrinos within a specific mass range, which explains why their three-flavor model is inconsistent. By incorporating axion-mediated neutrino interactions and utilizing a sum rule for neutrino magnetic moments, we establish that sterile neutrino masses in the range of MeV to eV are feasible. These interactions also stabilize a modulated neutrino mixture that can be probed through low-energy processes like the $6Li$ anomaly and the Reynolds number in fluid flows. Additionally, we demonstrate that the predicted scale of right-handed neutrino masses is within the range of the Peccei-Quinn scale and the GUT scale.

Quantum information processing relies heavily on precise control over quantum states and operations, and specifically, the use of magic states and their associated stabilizer forms has become a crucial concept in developing quantum algorithms and achieving advantage in specific tasks. However, the definition of these forms lacks explicit protocols for constructing the states, which hampers their practical implementation. Research has made significant progress in establishing explicit protocols based on quantum computation with few qubits, leading to upper bounds on the stabilizer rank of certain magic states and related objects. In the paper, we significantly improve these upper bounds in three key areas. Firstly, we establish a universal limit on the stabilizer rank of Haar-random mixed states of n qubits. Secondly, we demonstrate that the stabilizer rank of -states with d systems is capped at 2 to the power of cd^2, and thirdly, we show that the stabilizer rank of affine Pauli states with d systems is also capped at 2 to the power of cd^2.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in conjunction with the Essence model, derived from $\Lambda(CN)$-EM, to develop a modified scenario. We initially present the Swift-Like model, based on the interaction parameter, $f$,
with subsequent derivation of key equations. We utilize the junction condition to extract values for essential parameters, following which we analyze plots for embedding factors, $C$, and the parameter, $\gamma$, in relation to both space and time.

The LAMOST time-domain survey began conducting multi-epoch observations in July 2016 and has been ongoing for nearly five years. This program has successfully observed second-time baseline data for 550,111 stars and third-time baseline data for 236,171 stars. The first publication of LAMOST time-domain survey data has become available through the Vizier database. This includes information on stars with variable star labels, as well as their observational data. The publication also contains a study of 214 RR Lyrae, 121 DLGi, 79 Cepheid, 64 SX Phoenic and 38 Delta Scuti stars. Researchers found that RR Lyrae, Cepheid and SX Phoeni stars followed the expected relationships for their respective types. However, DLGi stars required a larger fraction of metallic elements to explain their behavior, while Delta Scuti stars needed a larger fraction of logarithmic gravity than expected. The study of RR Lyrae and Cepheid stars allowed researchers to determine the optical absolute magnitudes of these variables. The results from LAMOST time-domain survey data showed good agreement with other studies.

Previous research has suggested the potential for SRAM cells to generate random numbers by exploiting inherent data corruption caused by manufacturing variations and operating conditions, such as substrate noise, and allowing the extracted results to be post-processed through statistical analysis to obtain truly random data. However, past attempts to utilize SRAM-based random number generators have been hindered by low throughput and the need for complex computation. To address these limitations, this paper introduces TuRaN, a novel SRAM-based approach to generate random numbers quickly and efficiently by temporarily reducing the operating voltage to a fraction of the normal value and collecting data from SRAM cells before reinitializing them. By optimizing the trade-off between random number quality and energy consumption, TuRaN can generate high-quality random numbers 10-20 times faster than previous methods, often at a significantly lower energy cost.

We have designed a novel molecular nonvolatile single-electron resistor switch and examined its functioning using advanced computer simulations. Initially, two distinct molecular devices were proposed, one of which utilized a non-conductive molecule and showed single-electron resistance properties, whereas the other, based on a conductive molecule, exhibited a charge-trap mechanism following electron injection. However, the latter design proved unsuitable for all-molecular integrated circuits. To overcome limitations, we modified the design of the molecular devices to incorporate only two functional parts: a charge-trap site and a barrier region. Using a 2D Delaunay mesh for simulations, we modeled these structures and demonstrated single-electron resistance capabilities with acceptable current levels and operating voltages within integrated circuit scalability standards. Furthermore, our findings revealed the long-term stability of these molecular devices at 300K, enduring for 100 years in ambient conditions and 10 years in space applications.

A novel approach called LoopTools 2 is introduced, which utilizes causal structures to compute multi-loop Feynman integrals with particle production.  Building upon xTensor and CausalLink, this method expands the functionality of LoopTreeDecay by incorporating a range of advanced features. These enhancements include the determination of causal structures, loop integrands from causal structures, and loop integrals via Owen and XSpace. Additionally, a bubble resummation technique is integrated from Semiperturbative. Furthermore, a range of numerical and visualization tools from CausalLink are integrated. The development of LoopTools 2 is documented in detail, with a comprehensive set of examples also provided.

This paper presents a novel equation that describes one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, achieved through the repeated application of a specific evolution operator. By analyzing this equation, we derive conditions that ensure nonnegative probabilities for key transition elements, thereby demonstrating the convergence of a related series expansion. Furthermore, this analysis confirms that the walk's probability distribution can be accurately represented by the squared magnitude of a specific eigenfunction, corresponding to a well-known Stieltjes function.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho theoretical framework with two distinct equation-of-state models: MIT and NJL. The Sigma-omega-rho model incorporates three distinct vector mesons, each interacting with neutrons and protons in unique ways, while also mediating a significant repulsive force between these particles. Additionally, the model includes a repulsive correlation that becomes evident at high densities. In contrast, the NJL model solely focuses on color-dressed interactions between quarks, whereas the MIT bag model treats quarks as free, non-interacting particles within a confined space. The combination of these models yields hybrid stars consisting of quark cores and hadronic outer layers. Based on various mass threshold values, the maximum predicted masses of hybrid stars resulting from the MIT bag model stand at approximately 2.47 solar masses, while those resulting from the NJL model reach a maximum of 1.58 solar masses.

We explore the behavior of light interaction within a q-deformed optomechanical system. By leveraging the properties of the MX$_q$(2) matrix, a two-cavity system is analyzed for its general solution and properties of photon number, light transmission, and phase shift. Furthermore, we investigate how these properties are influenced by deformed parameters. Notably, we uncover instances of extreme light clarification and amplification within this system. Lastly, we examine the effects of deformed parameters on light transmission and phase shift.

In a model where an $SU(5)$ gauge symmetry breaks down into the Standard Model and a Wilson line, a two-rotors mechanism is proposed to explain the lack of R-parity as a dynamical process. This theory incorporates a $U(1)_B$ symmetry, which is responsible for generating Kuhn transformations and translating R-parity into B-parity. As an extension of this model, we've explored the behavior of R-parity vanishing modes within the Two-Rotors model. These non-existent R-parity states, which persist on the brane, can develop adverse characteristics when interacting with the bulk's B-parity symmetry, specifically in scenarios involving scissors modes on the Ericsson theorem spectrum.

This work delves into the phenomena of spin and orbital fluctuations in ultrathin films composed of transition-metal oxides, focusing on the underlying concepts and recent research findings.  It is established that these films exhibit unique and diverse properties that differ from their bulk counterparts, making them ideal for exploring new physical properties and functionalities.  Specifically, the interface with a substrate is shown to play a pivotal role in modifying the electronic properties, while interface dipoles and intermolecular interactions can significantly influence the ordering of electrons.  This is exemplified through the investigation of LaTiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ ultra-thin films, where distinct quantum phases arise due to the varying effective dimensions of electron orbital and spin fluctuations.  This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions underlying these phenomena and their potential for giving rise to novel phases with unique properties.

Recent findings have demonstrated that certain types of self-organizing systems, such as dissipative optical lattices, can be effectively described using unconventional statistical mechanics that accounts for elimination of particles. Building on this discovery, this study investigates fluctuations in number of atoms within a one-dimensional dissipative optical lattice as atoms are cooled by either an optical tweezers or a Lindblad master equation. Through in-depth analysis, this research demonstrates that, contrary to traditional assumptions, these fluctuations exhibit damped oscillations following a initial cooling event. Moreover, this study confirms that the steady-state fluctuations in such systems can be described using a well-established statistical method, whereas the immediate fluctuations post-cooling remain unpredictable and require further theoretical development.

This study examines the high-frequency data of cryptocurrency trading, investigating the diverse interactions among cryptocurrencies, their price correlations, and the impact on trading volumes. By employing a correlation-based network analysis, we identify the tight connections among cryptocurrencies, such as EOS with TRX and BTC. To explore the non-linear relationships, we constructed a multiplex network and discovered that the correlation strengths of each cryptocurrency vary. Analyzing the node centrality reveals that BTC holds the center stage in the cryptocurrency trading network, both in terms of correlation and trading volume. Furthermore, we found that the price of cryptocurrencies can be attributed to the combination of their individual characteristics and the interactions among them. To determine the optimal number of latent factors, we used different information criteria, ultimately confirming the validity of previous research findings.

The role of quantum fluctuations, or zero-point motion, in the formation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water is being investigated. The aim is to determine its significance by comparing the potential energy of classical and quantum states through the analysis of pair distribution functions. The study also examines the timescale at which quantum effects become prominent through the analysis of neutron scattering data and molecular dynamics simulations at different temperatures. The results indicate that quantum effects are most prominent at temperatures ranging from 180K to 220K, a region that corresponds to imminent particle formation.

We introduce CPPE, an efficient algorithm for compactifying high-dimensional data pairs and operator spaces, ensuring scalability for large datasets. The algorithm employs ADMM whitening and singular value projection to compactify each data pair, with a sample operator also projected, all within a group equivariance framework. The proposed method passes the so-called compatibility test, enabling stable results and computational efficiency. Tests on synthetic and real world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the method.

In quantum systems, the thermal Hall effect exhibits unique properties that significantly differ from their electromagnetic or gravitational counterparts. This distinct behavior is characterized by distinct dynamics when considering two or three non-compact extra dimensions. We demonstrate that this distinctiveness arises from the interaction between geometric curvature and quantum entanglement across space-like separations. Additionally, the thermal Hall effect's autonomous nature is highlighted by its insensitivity to gravitational dressing. Consequently, the typical relationships between flux, temperature, and curvature are not preserved, instead giving rise to more intricate, system-specific dependencies. These findings support the concept of distinct, non-equivalent branes in holographic duality, with potential implications for the study of complex quantum systems and their geometric invariants.

In various machine learning domains, it has been observed that overparameterized neural networks tend to avoid complex high-dimensional weight configurations, generalizing well even in scenarios where the training data is abundant. There are multiple theories attempting to explain this phenomenon, each highlighting a distinct aspect: regularization through early stopping, group sparsity and geometric complexity may contribute to this behavior. However, these different perspectives have not been integrated into a unified understanding until now. By dissecting the effects of forward loss gradient and backward backpropagation, we gain insights into how these components interact and propose a comprehensive framework that unifies previous explanations. Our model is supported by numerical experiments conducted across various loss functions, architectures, and feature dimensions.

A study on $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ four-body decays is carried out for the first time by analyzing data collected with the LHCb detector, equivalent to 3.0 ${\rm fb^{-1}}$ of $B^0$ decays into $K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$, including both prompt and in-flight decays of the $K^{*0}$. Wilson coefficients at low energies are determined directly through a fit that also accounts for potential variations in contributions from higher-order processes in the determination of these coefficients. The results are consistent with the findings of the ATLAS, CMS, CDF, D0 experiments for the $b\to s\ell^-\bar{\ell}^+$ processes, but a discrepancy with the CDF result for one specific coefficient has been noted, $C_7$. Additionally, upper limits on the coefficients $C_5-C_6,C_8-C_9,C_{10},C_{12}-C_{14}$ are established with a combined confidence level of 97.5%, while the CDF value of $C_7$ lies outside the 95.5% confidence level interval established in this study.

A prominent assessment tool, Automated Essay Scoring (AES), has been widely used to evaluate student performance in writing. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have particularly enhanced the effectiveness of AES systems based on language models. To counter class imbalance issues and improve model robustness, data enhancement techniques are commonly employed in deep learning applications. This research investigates the efficacy of three data enhancement methods - word replacement, sentence insertion, and text augmentation using a GPT-2 model - to improve the performance of AES systems based on transformer models. The study compares the performance of these methods and also examines the potential risks of using text augmentation for AES. The results show that word replacement and the GPT-2 method significantly boost the F1 score and precision of the AES system, while sentence insertion also improves performance but is also associated with certain drawbacks. The research finds that word replacement yields the best performance with minimal computational costs and recommends its use in future AES system development.

The paper focuses on flexible systems to analyze multivariate data by modeling individual variable relationships with others. It evaluates both theoretical and practical aspects of these systems. Theoretical analysis involves specifying conditions for consistent estimation and deriving limits for parameter estimation methods. Practically, it presents examples using simulated and real-world data to demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods.

A theoretical model, the Opportunity Fairness Model, is developed to examine how opportunities are distributed across different age groups in a dynamic setting with unpredictable birth rates and aging processes. This is achieved by converting the dynamic problem into an equivalent static one, involving graph theory and the study of fair allocations, whose solutions reveal various inequalities governing opportunity distribution. The model is further utilized to investigate the relationship between a society's structure and the way opportunities are distributed, as well as the effect of aging on this distribution. Lastly, a novel concept, called "opportunity fairness," is introduced to assess the overall fairness of allocating opportunities to ensure a level playing field for future generations.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded version of RingCT with enhanced performance, maintaining the same level of security as the original scheme. The current RingCT method used in Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS) blockchain technologies suffers from prolonged transaction validation time, necessitating a security patch to ensure the continued stability of the network. The revised RingCT technique addresses these issues by applying a combination of computational and information-theoretic security to achieve the desired level of security, combined with an efficient delegation mechanism. The primary advantages of this new method are the removal of unnecessary security assumptions and a significant reduction in computational complexity, which in turn minimizes transaction processing time and allows for increased transaction processing capacity.

We examine the computational resilience of linear system solvers on various architectures, focusing on the impact of hardware vulnerabilities affecting memory safety. A theoretical model determines the solvers' toughness in addressing corrupted or manipulated memory, which is corroborated through practical tests on Linux-based systems utilizing the Armv8 architecture. Moreover, our findings showcase the inherent versatility of inverse-free iterative methods in safeguarding against memory-related threats, which we further illustrate with the development of a highly resilient solver for symmetric positive definite matrices implemented in the LAPACK library.

The production of three highly energetic bosons, specifically $W$ or $Z$ particles, is thoroughly examined in both proton-proton and lead-lead collisions. These events are analyzed based on a theoretical model that incorporates the latest quantum chromodynamics (QCD) principles. The predictions for $pp$ collisions at 13 TeV are made precise, accounting for all relevant higher-order processes. The findings for $W$ production are compared with data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments, demonstrating a strong match. Additionally, production cross-sections of $WWZ$ and $ZZZ$ particles in $pp$ collisions are calculated, along with an exploration of the production of $W$ or $Z$ particles in association with a high number of hard jets. The production of $W$ or $Z$ particles in lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV is examined, taking into account the effects of temperature and density. These effects are modeled with the EPOS LHC parameterization, allowing a comparison with a parameterization based on the collective behavior of particles.

Hebrew, the most spoken language in Israel, lacks adequate NLP resources, which hinders advancements in the field. To address this gap, a new UD treebank was developed using data from the Israeli National Health Records. This paper discusses the motivations, benefits, and methodology of the new treebank. To ensure accuracy, the annotation process was double-checked by experienced linguists. The project also includes UD annotations for 10,000 sentences from various natural language texts. Additionally, a parallel annotation was performed for 4,000 sentences from Israeli news articles. The new treebank was used to demonstrate state-of-the-art parsing results using modern transformer-based models. The full dataset and associated models are available for download at https://he UD.github.io.

We establish that for linear operators T and S, and positive real numbers epsilon and one, there exists a dimension decrease for incompressible subsets of ell_p spaces such that applying T to this subset results in an epsilon-isometric image within an altered subset of the original. This dimension decrease is represented by a bound on the cardinality of the altered subset in relation to the original, which is greater than epsilon to the power of p, divided by two. Our research generalizes a previous finding from Davidson and Zhang to ell_p spaces, and we specifically demonstrate that for ell_2, the epsilon-isometric dimension decrease can be achieved with a dependence on epsilon to the power of four, and that this is optimal. Furthermore, we prove that our general result is also applicable to the ell_p spaces of p values between one and two, by utilising distinct techniques for p values greater than two.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have led to a surge in using collaborative models to share knowledge across different datasets, projects, and domains. However, the application of collaborative models is often hindered by a variety of obstacles: data discrepancies, missing or incomplete information, and differing data quality, to name a few. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to overcome these hurdles by leveraging the power of learning from multiple sources of data simultaneously. We develop a set of data-driven methods to construct a collaborative model from disparate datasets, each described by a varying number of parameters, and subsequently refine it through iterative iterations of model sharing and parameter adjustment. We validate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to the analysis of synthetic and real-world chromatin conformation data, and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods under a variety of scenarios.

Current research on error correction using codes on the binary deletion channel assumes code symbols to be independently deleted. However, analyzing the scenario where multiple adjacent code symbols are deleted is essential, particularly since neighboring code symbols often share edges in a density stability graph representing a low-density parity-check code. We combine techniques from density stability and degree-degree distributions to develop new bounds for low-density parity-check codes aimed at preventing density stability failures under the binary deletion channel. Our research further introduces degree-degree correlated Gallager codes and demonstrates the effectiveness of these codes in achieving improved error correction performance compared to conventional Gallager codes.

Modern software applications require a multi-faceted approach to address various security threats, including protection from malicious code injection, unauthorized data access, and tampering via bit manipulation. The challenge lies in designing a comprehensive security framework that is efficient, adaptable, and applicable across different platforms, without being cumbersome to use. Traditional methods face this dilemma by mixing security techniques and implementing complex custom solutions. This paper proposes a novel security framework that efficiently combines multiple security techniques, offering a lightweight and easy-to-use solution for securing software applications and embedded systems. The framework, dubbed SecSLIM, leverages system-level synthesis to merge secure translation, integrity checking, and unwrapping techniques, yielding a highly efficient and adaptable system capable of handling diverse security threats. SecSLIM can be applied to software and hardware components, providing seamless integration across various platforms and enabling a smooth security framework for application developers.

A critical component in quantum key distribution (QKD) systems is the source, which our research focuses on - a fast and stable source designed to support multiple real-world QKD protocols. However, we identified a vulnerability in this source, which can be exploited to compromise its security. Specifically, we determined that randomly modulating the phase of field states can be insufficient in preventing a potential attack. Instead, the system's security can be breached if the randomization process is limited to a certain portion of the phases, leading to a significant reduction in the system's key distribution rate and long-term stability. To address this issue, we propose three potential solutions to enhance the system's security and mitigate the risk of being hacked.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their reliance on a single pretraining corpus limits scalability and real-world applicability. We conducted an in-depth examination of the impact of pretraining corpora on the learning performance of a 1.3 billion parameter LLM. Our analysis revealed that changing the pretraining corpus alters the model's output, making it difficult to achieve satisfactory results when working with unfamiliar datasets. Cross-domain generalization is also hindered by the issues above and is further exacerbated by the differences in writing styles and standards between the pretraining and test datasets. To address these problems, we propose a simple yet effective approach that combines multiple pretraining corpora. Our method employs a weighted ensemble of the model's outputs, where the weights are optimized through a standardized procedure. Our experimental results show that our approach significantly improves learning performance and accelerates convergence, ultimately facilitating reliable in-context learning and few-shot adaptation in a wide range of datasets.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the dynamics of central clusters, leaving the formation and evolution of their vast, diffuse clouds unknown. This research employed idealized simulations to model the growth and dissolution of these clouds, incorporating processes such as radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal energy transfer. The results showed that cooling and magnetic fields control the development of clouds, while thermal energy transfer primarily affects gas movement. The presence of magnetic fields significantly delayed the formation of high-density regions, while cool clouds only appear with strong fields - ultimately determining the structure and quantity of these features. The rate of cloud creation and destruction was found to be linked - when clouds form, they inevitably break down, and vice versa. Initially, the balance between growth and dissolution determined the long-term stability of clouds, primarily influenced by the rate of cooling, and to a lesser extent, of thermal energy transfer. The presence of magnetic fields significantly prolonged the life of clouds, primarily by slowing down the effects of cooling, and to a lesser extent, of thermal energy transfer.

The discovery of CP violation in beauty and charm systems over the past few decades has been a significant breakthrough in understanding fundamental physics. Current data on CP violation in beauty mesons, analysed using the T' matrix, reveals inconsistencies at the 3.3 sigma level that need further examination. If confirmed, this could point to the presence of new physics beyond the Standard Model. Notably, searches for CP violation in beauty decays have reached a level of sensitivity that can effectively test the predictions of the electroweak theory under conditions of strong interactions, offering a crucial test of the theory's internal consistency. Future research will focus on resolving this issue, which is essential for refining our understanding of fundamental physics.

We've calculated ten-dimensional open superstring scattering amplitudes for processes considered difficult to calculate directly. These processes involve bosons and high-energy collisions, and by using a relationship between these amplitudes and those in four dimensions, we've determined that a certain pattern exists in the mathematical representation of these processes. Specifically, we've found that a certain ratio between the four-dimensional and ten-dimensional amplitudes remains constant, even as the momentum of the particles involved increases. This finding confirms a hypothesis first proposed by Gross in 1988.

To manage increasing mobile data traffic in urban areas, mobile operators are shifting from traditional macro-cellular networks to more efficient distributed antenna systems (DAS). These can be achieved through different configurations such as active DAS (eNodeB in the street, user equipment connects to street node) or active hybrid DAS (eNodeB in the street, user equipment connects directly to eNodeB without going through street node). This research paper focuses on the required operations management systems for eNB-based DAS deployments, discussing the related challenges and possible solutions. It also proposes a set of standard procedures for administering these systems, exemplified through a case study involving a macro-layer that supports a DAS layer. The outcome of this research aligns with the goals of software-defined radio and future-proof networks by ensuring compatibility and equal treatment of different radio access technologies over the same core network interface.

The objective of zero-speech voice synthesis is to create a vocal version of text without relying on annotated speech data. Previous studies achieved partial success in this area, but the quality of the synthesized speech remained inferior to speech units trained on large speech corpora. This research proposes an alternative approach that utilizes short, duration-sensitive acoustic units called "phonons," which are identified through a dynamic and efficient transcription process called "phononization." Phonons are defined as the most distinctive phonetic components present in a speech signal. To minimize transcription errors, phononization benefits from both suprasegmental context prediction and fine-grained waveform prediction. The predicted transcripts are then used to define the phonons, which are subsequently modeled using a variant of the Vocoder called "Phonotrance." The synthesis pipeline includes a residual model trained on phonon sequences, which generates a more detailed signal. Evaluations demonstrate that the proposed phonon-based approach outperforms state-of-the-art zero-speech voice synthesis methods in terms of both objective metrics and human listening tests.

The subject of motion planning via parameter optimization has become increasingly prevalent in the field. A novel multi-stage optimization framework, centered on McCormick envelope relaxations, is introduced to tackle this issue. By leveraging data-driven insights during the initial training phase, tight linear relaxations are obtained, enabling the development of an effective and efficient algorithm. Through stage-wise updates, the computational burden is minimized, allowing for rapid online implementation. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this approach over competing methods, showcasing its capacity to accurately plan motions while maintaining a low online solving time.

A fundamental concept in quantum thermodynamics, probabilistic convertibility, enables us to analyze the practical applications of quantum states, despite inaccessibility of exact conversions. By employing the least restrictive approach, the minimum required probability for converting a given quantum state into another involves a computable formula that factors in their relative multiplicities and the minimum amount of entropy exchanged during the process. Furthermore, we investigate stricter forms of probabilistic convertibility, such as achieving the maximum probability, which is always computable and within a specified range, and ensuring the entire process occurs with a single, fixed probability. These stricter constraints offer valuable insights into the inherent characteristics of relative multiplicities in quantum systems and provide a comprehensive classification of different types of multiplicities based on their mathematical properties.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a mathematical model that represents a forced pendulum with its plane aligned diagonally. The parameters of mass, gravity, and moment of inertia determine the natural frequency of the pendulum, which can also be influenced by its position. When excited, the system undergoes a general movement that can be analyzed through a combination of normal modes and resonances. The average angular velocity of the cup, caused by its movement, is considered as a constant input in the system, resulting in a steady state characterized by a persistent angular movement. The observed angular movements can vary from small rotations to nearly a half rotation, depending on the characteristics of the normal modes and the intensity of the excitation.

In the context of decentralized over-comeable optimization over graph topologies, we develop a novel algorithm, DR-DSGD, to tackle complex non-convex problems. By incorporating the concept of distributional robustness from $f$-divergence into the traditional Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD), we design and analyze DR-DSGD. We derive a quantitative relationship for the first time, ensuring its almost sure convergence under certain conditions. Furthermore, we investigate the robustness of DR-DSGD by quantitatively linking its performance to the standard DSGD under specific control parameters. We test DR-DSGD's efficacy on various real-world datasets and compare it to the original DSGD algorithm, demonstrating improved resilience and faster convergence in several scenarios.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions.
