By validating our model with actual incident data, we demonstrate its effectiveness and accuracy in identifying various types of incidents across different test cases.

Our study focuses on examining the radiative and sequential decays of the $X(3872)$, specifically investigating its transition into $J/\psi$ accompanied by a photon or a photon and charged pions, with a focus on understanding the underlying internal structure of the $X(3872)$. By utilizing an effective Lagrangian derived from its theoretical description as an $S$-wave $D^*D\pi$ molecule and $Z(3930)$, our analysis ultimately derives theoretical branching ratio limits for these decays and relates them to the wave function mass distribution of the $X(3872)$.

We provide a comprehensive description of quadric surfaces within the context of 3-dimensional projective geometry, emphasizing its categorical formulation. This approach describes quadrics through their association with self-dual mutations of Gorenstein algebras, thereby offering a comprehensive understanding of their linear series and line configurations. Additionally, this framework allows us to classify line configurations of quadrics, resulting in a comprehensive enumeration of their varieties.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 30 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to generate text on the fly.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a high-performance game engine built using modern technologies to achieve a remarkable increase in processing speed of over 30 times that of existing text-based games, enabling a million actions per second and allowing large-scale agent testing.

We develop a comprehensive mathematical framework to describe topological insulators with defects. Our approach is grounded in $A$-mathematics, utilizing $\mathbb{A}$-modules from $A$-categories. Through $\mathbb{A}$-functorial methods, we establish operators for surface states on insulators with boundary defects. By integrating MeX-operators, we generalize the bulk-spectrum decomposition theorem to accommodate defects. Further, we explore the application of quivers and $\mathbb{A}$-representations to model both internal and external symmetries, while examining the closure of the insulator's spectrum via $\mathbb{A}$-inclusions.

Consider a set of positive measure $\Sigma$ within the complex plane, and a function $u$ that is $p$-harmonic ($1 < p < \infty$) in $\Sigma$ and subharmonic in its complex dilation by a factor of $k$. We demonstrate that for any point $z_0$ located in $\Sigma$ and not on its boundary, the following growth estimate holds: there exists a constant $C$, dependent on $u$, $\Sigma$, and $k$, such that $|u(z) - u(z_0)| \leq C|1-\langle z, z_0 \rangle|^\frac{1}{p-1}$, where the norm is $p$-norm, and $z$ is a point in the set $\{z \in \Sigma : |z-wz_0| < dist(z_0, \partial \Sigma)\}$. This is analogous to a result by Vodop'yanov that held for $p=2$. We also establish that for functions that are $p$-harmonic in sectors, a mean value inequality holds, and this in turn leads to Liouville-type theorems for quasilinear polyharmonic functions in the complex plane. If the function $u$ is also harmonic in its complex dilation by a factor of $k$, and $1 < p < \infty$, and the set $\Sigma$ has an interior

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between weather system types, joint occurrence of extremes, and spatial relationships is examined for extreme weather patterns in the North East Atlantic Ocean. The model is applied with weather system types identified through a clustering analysis of Atlantic depressions and their associated spatial characteristics, as determined by a principal component analysis. The results suggest that the model effectively captures spatial and temporal relationships, including the occurrence of univariate extremes and uncorrelated patterns of multivariate extremes.

We establish a general finitude theorem for non-constant morphisms from affine curves defined over number fields to projective spaces, by combining Tschirnhaus results with an alternative version of Tschirnhaus with rational coefficients. This yields an estimate of $3g+2$ for curves of genus $g$, aligning with Tschirnhaus's order for function fields. Furthermore, we derive a separate estimate for maps from curves of higher genus, influenced by Igusa's inequality. This study also explores the scavenger hunt problem for non-constant maps in a more comprehensive context.

A significant advancement in using learned manipulator skills directly in a planning context, known as a planning-based manipulability domain, has made it possible to leverage the power of planning. This approach effectively treats a manipulator as part of the state space, infusing the planning context with manipulability information. However, this method relies on naive state equivalence assumptions that don't hold up when dealing with diverse robot designs. This research introduces an original method to compare and equate states across different robots, drawing on concepts from differential geometry. Specifically, it employs parallel transport to estimate the manipulability gradient on a manifold of achievable states. Additionally, it develops a manifolds-aware Iterative Closest Point algorithm to estimate a robot's end-effector position based on incomplete pointcloud data. This method demonstrates superior performance in state estimation and planning tasks involving uncertainty and partial observability. You can access the paper at this link: https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS40201.2021.9637501

In a study of Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ process at the LHC, we examine how to apply the matrix element method using simulated events. Specifically, we investigate the outcomes of parton shower Monte Carlo methods and find that some variations significantly alter the predictions, allowing for the determination of production rates with uncertainties ranging from 30% to 300%. These findings inform the analysis strategy for determining Higgs boson pair production cross sections in the $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D pose estimation models, which leverages short video clips where objects' rotational intentions are incidental to their primary purposes. It utilizes these 'Accidental Turntables' to enhance existing 3D pose models through few-shot fine-tuning, thereby improving their performance and reducing reliance on lengthy video data collections. Additionally, the method proposes TurntableCAP, a model that directly predicts 3D pose from a single image by incorporating the analysis of turntable motions, demonstrating improved results compared to existing models.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial portion of the population remains skeptical due to social media influencing people's beliefs about vaccines' safety. Misinformation disseminated through platforms like Twitter plays a significant role in fostering anti-vaccination sentiments. To address this issue, we propose a novel task that aims to distinguish accepting or rejecting attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation expressed on Twitter. We have compiled a dataset of 2,379 English tweets and their corresponding user comments, which serve as the foundation for our research. By experimenting with various models and data representations, we have found that a combination of learning approaches - including fine-tuning BERT and self-supervised negative sampling - yields optimal performance. Notably, our model achieves a high accuracy of 85.5% on an independent test set, demonstrating the effectiveness of pre-trained models and a proprietary data construction method in resolving this complex task.

We have demonstrated the ability to control attosecond pulse generation in a strong-field laser interaction through careful manipulation of its parameters. By strategically changing the laser's polarization, we can modulate the high-energy electron recollision event that produces the attosecond pulse, essentially "regulating" its intensity. This research uses the three-step model to examine how altering the strong-field laser parameters affects the attosecond pulse, revealing a previously unexplored mechanism to control recollision via polarization. This discovery offers a pathway to increase attosecond pulse intensity and achieve greater control over their properties.

Eclipse star systems typically involve three core components: a main inner object, a main outer object, and in most cases, a third sensitive object. Historically, the inner object has usually been a low or intermediate mass star, whereas the third sensitive object has been a black hole or a neutron star. Notably, however, there is a notable lack of detected cases where the third sensitive object is a white dwarf, even though such situations should theoretically occur with a frequency of around 70% according to existing models. Researchers recently analyzed a list of prime candidates for systems involving an eclipse and a mysterious third component, and as a result, increased the total count of systems potentially involving a low mass inner object and a white dwarf as the third component by a factor of around 3. These newly identified candidates show characteristics common in such systems, and through their analysis, researchers provided a new boundary for the overall white dwarf mass in such systems, and detected a notable imbalance in detected systems involving a low mass inner object and a black hole as the third component.

We demonstrate the existence of explosive solutions to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation under a specified potential in a specific region of Euclidean space. These explosive solutions occur when initial conditions with sufficient energy and momentum are given as time approaches negative infinity. Notably, we find that a potential with negative coefficient is sufficient, but it must be less than a certain value that depends on additional constants. This research extends our previous findings on solutions in a specific type of periodic environment and provides evidence of explosive behavior in a region of Euclidean space.

Recently, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have gained attention for estimating derivatives of functions, particularly due to their robustness in incorporating physical laws and limited data. The key component of a PINN is a neural network with nodes that produce output values. Typically, a PINN uses an evenly spaced input domain with a fixed number of nodes to achieve results. However, this approach has limitations as it may not adequately capture boundary conditions and is sensitive to overfitting when working with partial differential equations (PDEs). To address these limitations, we introduce a new adaptive node creation method called RANG (Residual-based Adaptive Node creation using Gaussian processes), which dynamically positions nodes based on residual errors of approximated solutions and effectively increases the number of nodes to prevent overfitting. The proposed method is computationally efficient, easy to implement, and significantly improves approximation quality compared to existing methods when solving both linear and nonlinear PDEs.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of a multi-domain ferroelectric FET by analyzing its electrostatic characteristics. We began by validating the effectiveness of a 1D Ritz model in calculating domain wall induced capacitance across various bias settings. Following the model's verification, we performed a detailed analysis of how changes in domain wall states and boundary positions affect a bi-domain FeFET's gate-to-channel capacitance. We found that a mere 10nm shift in the boundary can result in a 2 orders of magnitude increase in the Cdd component. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that domain wall movement can result in the development of significant charge, which in turn impacts device performance. We also explored the impact of domain wall related issues on circuit levels, expecting a notable increase in noise and variability.

Modern cargo ecosystems rely heavily on third-party dependencies, exposing them to security risks via vulnerability propagation.  This propagation can cause significant damage, as seen in recent events like Eventide, which compromised nearly 20% of Node.js projects.  To combat this issue, we developed CEDD, a knowledge graph that tracks dependency updates and vulnerability information.  CEDD allows for the analysis of cargo ecosystem weakness propagation by identifying vulnerable paths and experimentally validating propagation rates.  By categorizing vulnerabilities and studying their propagation, we found that half of cargo dependencies are weakened, with 6.4% of versions affected.  Additionally, we found that cargo developers take 3 days to address weaknesses, with 25% of versions unchanged after 200 days.  Our research concludes that cargo vulnerability propagation is a pressing issue that requires more attention from the maintenance community to prevent further damage.

We demonstrate that in a fixed time period, the stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation driven by leap noise from an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is irreducible, provided the nonlinear interaction term does not equal one. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinear term does not equal one, we find that in a fixed time period, solutions to the stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation driven by leap noise are unique and depend continuously on the initial conditions, thus establishing the global well-posedness of these solutions.

This research paper focuses on determining the minimum vertex degree of the power graph associated with each finite nilpotent group of a particular class, a concept first introduced by Ali, Das, and Kokarev in 2021. By examining the maximal nilpotent subgroups of finite nilpotent groups, we are able to establish the minimum vertex degree of their power graphs. Additionally, we derive minimum possible values for the clique number and chromatic number of power graphs associated with specific types of finite nilpotent groups.

HADES is an internal particle detector at the GSI Darmstadt, specifically designed to study the properties of heavily produced particles in nuclear physics experiments. With the ability to detect particles at various angles, HADES has a detection threshold of approximately 0.2 GeV/c for charged particles and 0.5 GeV/c for neutral particles, allowing it to study a wide range of topics. These include hyperons produced in proton-proton and proton-lead collisions, vector mesons created in nuclear collisions at the LHCp, and cosmic-ray induced events at high energies. This report outlines the detector's design and detection capabilities.

Direction convolution networks (DCNs) efficiently perform standard convolution operations by utilizing directional weight patterns and calculating dot products along these directions. In theory, DCNs with various directions of weight symmetry can achieve comparable results to standard convolution networks. In practice, we found that diagonal direction convolution networks (DDCNs) performed well in image recognition tasks and demonstrated advantages over standard convolution networks in terms of reduced parameters, increased receptive fields, and improved results. Additionally, we explored the potential of combining DDCNs with residual blocks to enhance their effectiveness. Our experiments showed that pre-trained DDCNs could be effectively fine-tuned for image recognition tasks, resulting in improved performance over commonly used methods.

This study delves into the key elements of graph convolutional networks' (GCNs) functionality in point cloud learning, including the construction of spatial neighbourhood domains, multi-layer network fusion, and parameter tuning. It examines how these components interact and influence the performance of GCNs in downstream tasks. Based on empirical observations, it is found that GCNs are prone to overfitting due to overlapping neighbourhood domains and the combination of features from different layers, which can negate each other. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed that selectively incorporates features from different layers and adjusts the size of spatial neighbourhood domains. Compared to existing methods, the proposed framework achieves better performance and requires fewer parameters.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses the inherent semantics in neural networks to deceive classifiers without requiring access to model parameters. Our proposed attack method can be applied to classifiers without being altered itself, making it a 'host-less' attack. In contrast to existing Trojan attacks, which rely on backdoors embedded in model parameters, our approach employs neural network semantics to craft backdoors. Our experiments demonstrate that the semantic Trojan attack possesses comparable stealthiness and generality capabilities compared to the backdoor Trojan attack, while also exhibiting enhanced generalization abilities and adaptability to diverse classifier architectures and input distributions.

We are introducing an imaging fiber bundle for the Magellan IMACS spectrograph at the Las Campanas Observatory. The device, titled ROSIE (Reliable Optimal Spectrograph Income to Evolving databases), will serve as an option for broad-band, multi-object spectroscopy with a unique approach to field coverage and spectral coverage. The device will enable researchers to target up to 250 objects across 450 different slits, each with a slitlet width of 1.5", spanning a field of view 20" in diameter. The distance between the slits is 8", with the sledge able to hold 10 different setups, each with a field of view. The device will allow observations of extended sources, including galaxies, star-forming regions, and active galactic nuclei, as well as various astrophysical targets. The device will offer multiple options for spectral range and resolution, with a maximum resolution of 4200 and spectral range of 350nm to 680nm. The device will soon undergo its final integration and testing phase.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, the paper discusses key advancements in the Trojan Horse Method, enabling the precise measurement of low-energy astrophysical $S$-factors without being influenced by non-resonant background reactions. The enhancement of the THM's sensitivity to specific resonances allows for the accurate extraction of astrophysical $S$-factors for significant barriers under constant astrophysical conditions. Based on the most recent THM measurements and theoretical estimates, it is concluded that the standard model of low-energy astrophysical $S$-factors is upheld, but the direct measurement of these values at depths below the Coulomb barrier is necessary for a thorough understanding of the threshold behavior.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies focus on elements like C, N, O, which are essential for understanding a planet's interior composition and mass. Researchers have developed an accurate method for measuring these elements in stars hosting terrestrial planets by correlating their abundances with core properties. Utilizing this approach, the team has determined the core radii and mass fractions of 55 Cen b, GJ 367 b, and GJ 673 b. The core radius of 55 Cen b is estimated at 1.6-3.1 Earth radii ($R_{\Earth}$), containing 10-40% of its mass. For GJ 367 b and GJ 673 b, core radius estimates range from 1.1-2.9 $R_{\Earth}$ with 5-30% of their mass. These core measurements can be compared with data from NASA's InSight lander on Mars, providing further insights into Martian core characteristics.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become the preferred method for wireless localization using channel state information (CSI), outperforming previous approaches due to their ability to effectively extract CSI features for location purposes. However, effectively combining CSI features with spatial relationships between nodes remains a difficult task, leading to lower accuracy in location estimation. To address this, this research introduces an attention mechanism to assist existing CSI-based localization DNNs, allowing them to better communicate CSI features and spatial relationships between nodes, ultimately resulting in improved location estimation accuracy. The proposed approach can be applied to various DNN architectures without significantly increasing computational complexity, as it involves simply stacking convolutional layers and attention mechanisms. The research demonstrates that introducing the attention mechanism yields a 8.11% average gain in location estimation accuracy over baseline DNNs.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logics by categorically extending Kripke models to their topological equivalents, thereby unifying and systematizing existing approaches. It includes a range of standard modal logics as subcases, offering a unified perspective on these logics through the relationship between their structures (topological structures) and their semantic frameworks (topological categories). Building on this framework, the paper explores key properties within each category, specifically examining the role of modal operators as topological homotopy classes and their connection to the category theory formulation of substructural logics.

A graph's edge coloring is defined as the minimum number of colors required to color edges such that no two adjacent edges have the same color. We specifically looked into the maximum degree of a graph and how it relates to edge coloring, particularly searching for a function f that satisfies the condition Δ(G) ≤ f(n) and n/f(n) → 2, but found a counterexample in the form of a bipartite cubic graph, specifically the Johnson graph J(6, 3), which does not meet the criteria for a certain function f, and thus does not meet the criteria for a certain property related to edge coloring. We also looked into a related problem, finding the minimum number of colors needed for a bipartite cubic graph, and provided a lower bound in the form of (n/3) + (n/6) + (n/6) ~ (1/2) n. We then looked into the related problem of finding the minimum number of colors needed for a cubic bipartite graph, and provided a lower bound in the form of (n/3) + (n/6) + (n/6) ~ (1/2) n. We specifically searched for a function f such that n/ f(n) → 2, and found that J(6, 3) provides a counterexample to such a function. We then looked into the related problem of finding the minimum number of colors needed for a bipartite cubic

This study explores the minimum eigenvalue of the normalized Laplacian of the Hamming graph H(n, q) for n ≥ 2 and q ≥ 2, focusing on the normalized Laplacian's lower bound. When q equals 2, the lower bound is determined by a simple formula in terms of n. For q greater than 2, the problem is re-framed as a linear programming problem, and its constraints are linked to the eigenvalues of a specific graph, ultimately yielding a minimum eigenvalue expression for H(n, q) when q is greater than or equal to 3. Additionally, the study examines the minimum eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix of H(n, q), revealing a minimum eigenvalue expression that depends on both n and q. Notably, this research draws upon the properties of the bipartite K(q, q) graph and its connection to the bipartite dual of the Johnson graph J(n, q).

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless navigation. Leveraging RStudio Connect's deployment capabilities, ShinyCOPASI can be hosted on public or private servers, enhancing accessibility and security. Designed for running on powerful servers, ShinyCOPASI offers efficient large-scale simulations and data analysis across the web. Additionally, users can launch local COPASI sessions from the web interface by clicking a button.

Scientific machine learning has accelerated the pace of discovery by leveraging computational power to analyze expansive datasets and complex systems. As SML models gain trust in their ability to learn from data, there's a growing need to evaluate their reliability. This research delves into existing methods for quantifying uncertainty in SML models, grouping them into four categories: aggregation, modification, combining with prior knowledge, and learning from uncertain inputs. The study introduces a standardized framework for comparing uncertainty metrics and conducts an in-depth analysis with a diverse set of benchmarks. Findings suggest that certain metrics excel across a range of tasks, while others show potential for further improvement. This research aims to provide a reference point for practitioners navigating the uncertainty measures available in the literature.

We are investigating the closure of the set of category functions on a compact quantum group, denoted as ${\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)$. The paper provides functional inequalities that define a von Neumann algebra containing ${\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)$. The study also involves identifying a subalgebra within this larger algebra and computing its relative atomicity. Specifically, we demonstrate that the closure of ${\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)$ is a subset of $M_{2p^\!*}({\mathcal B}^{\mathrm{op}}\overline{\Delta})'$. Moreover, we define a subalgebra $({\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)\otimes {\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H))_s$ as the closure of $(x\otimes y)s$ for all $x,y\in {\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H), s\in S$. We prove that this subalgebra has relative atomicity equal to $\frac{1}{2p^\!*} M_{2p^\!*}({\mathcal B}^{\mathrm{op}}\overline{\Delta})'$.

Markov decision processes (MDPs) are resolved through policy iteration, a iterative algorithm that produces optimal policies for given reward functions. However, standard iterative methods face issues when dealing with large-scale MDPs due to their tendency to converge slowly or even worse, oscillate indefinitely. To address these limitations, researchers introduced the generalized Markov decision processes (GMDPs), a theoretical framework that ensures stable and precise convergence in GMDPs. Nonetheless, dealing with large-scale GMDPs remains impractical because of the computational expense involved. To overcome these constraints, researchers introduced the generalised iterative method (GM) for large-scale finite GMDPs, but it requires an excessively large number of operations. To make GMDPs applicable in real-world scenarios, the researchers introduced an interval version of the GM method (IGM) that provides an approximate solution within predetermined time constraints. The IGM method guarantees a precise solution if the approximate one intersects the optimal solution, with the distance between them bounded. The researchers developed an implementation of the IGM method, referred to as imprecise GM method (IGM), for solving large-scale finite GMDPs. To accelerate convergence, researchers introduced an acceleration technique (AT) based on an inexact generalized residual method (GMRES) and observed a substantial speed-up in the (IGM+AT) method. The researchers evaluated the (IGM+AT) method through numerical experiments and noted that it usually terminates after a relatively small number of iterations. The computational

Let $G$ be a weighted oriented graph. The edge ideal $I(G)$ and its $k$-th typical power $I^{(k)}(G)$ are defined. It is demonstrated that for every weighted oriented graph $G$, the edge ideal has the property that $I^{(k)}(G)$ is contained in the symbolic $k$-th power of $I(G)$, given by $I(G)[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$. Additionally, it is shown that for quadratic edge ideals, the inclusions $I^{(k)}(G) \subseteq \sqrt{I(G)}^k$ and $I(G)[X_1,\ldots,X_n] \subseteq \sqrt{I(G)}^k$ are true. This verification resolves an open issue from a previous study.

To direct computer simulators, users must feed them input and obtain output in the form of time series data. When a large number of experimental runs are necessary, processing this data can be time-consuming, leading to a significant bottleneck in the testing process. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a new method to quickly obtain optimal input settings for computer simulators, which produces high-quality output in a relatively short time. Building on existing techniques, this approach employs a specialized algorithm to analyze the simulators' behavior and identify key patterns in the data. By breaking down the simulators' responses into distinct regions, or contours, this estiamtor identifies the most relevant patterns and uses them to produce an accurate map, or surface, that summarizes the simulators' behavior. To validate this approach, researchers tested it using real-world data from a pharmaceutical company, which was able to provide a precise description of the simulators' behavior using only a small number of samples. Additionally, this algorithm was able to find an optimal input setting that the original simulator could use to produce high-quality output, which it was otherwise unable to do.

This study investigates the role of local inquiries in enhancing robustness in machine learning, focusing on adversarial robustness. We contribute novel insights into the beneficial effects of local inquiries and related constraints, drawing on concepts from information theory and geometry. Our findings reveal that local inquiries are particularly useful when the underlying model has inherent limitations in distinguishing between adjacent points in the input space. These insights lead to the development of a theoretical framework, which guides the design of inquiry-based learning algorithms and evaluates their robustness advantages. Empirical support for our theory is demonstrated through experiments on standard image classification benchmarks, with the results suggesting that local inquiries can improve adversarial robustness while reducing training complexity.

For understanding how high-momentum jets interact with hot, dense media in heavy-ion collisions, this research uses ROOT to analyze data from the CMS experiment at the LHC. By collaborating with MIT, researchers investigated changes in jet fragmentation using isolated photons as a reference point. In peripheral collisions, they observed altered fragmentation patterns, specifically decreased yields of most sub-jets and increased totals yields across all sub-jets, compared to proton-proton collisions. Unlike central collisions, peripheral collisions exhibit a distinct 'alteration landscape', suggesting distinct media interactions.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of evaluating Apéry-type inverse binomial series with alternating signs. Such a series features hypergeometric functions with alternating signs in their numerator and denominator. We build upon previous findings by extending the range of values for $m$ and $n$ in the series, where both are greater than or equal to $2$. The calculation of these series values is connected to colored multiple zeta functions through an interesting relationship.

We have gathered additional near-infrared photometry for WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, revealing it to be an extremely cool brown dwarf with an estimated effective temperature of 102 to 145 Kelvin, situated about 16.7 light-years away. This measurement aligns with spectral features and uncertainty estimates from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer mission's spectral templates. Our analysis suggests the object is likely a low-mass brown dwarf with a mass in the range of 6.6 to 31 times that of Jupiter. This brown dwarf is thought to be a free-floating member of the Tucana-Horologium moving group, with an estimated age of 24 million years. This group is thought to be part of a larger complex that includes the Columba and CrA-Cor stone star clusters, all sharing a common origin and direction of motion. This is the sixth member of the THA group that has been identified through the all-sky Brown dwarf Catalogue, and the most distant, with a relatively cool temperature of 102-145K, and a low mass limit for a planet.

This letter describes the production of various hadrons, including pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons, in Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon of 5.44 TeV. The data were collected with the ALICE detector at the LHC, which has a high precision for momentum measurement, particularly in the central rapidity area. The production rates of these particles, especially in the mid-rapidity region, are closely related to the thermalization of the formed quark-gluon plasma and serve as a crucial indicator of viscosity in these high-energy collisions.

We've developed a novel approach to solving DGLAP equations for parton distribution functions by combining neural networks with renormalization group properties. By matching the NNPDF 3.1 PDFs, our neural networks are able to accurately evolve back to the PDF definition at a initial scale of $Q^2 = 25\,$ GeV$^2$. Furthermore, our method enables the extension of parton distribution functions to higher-dimensional distributions, such as those involving transverse momentum or color correlations, without introducing any additional complexity.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and were fired between 900-1200°C to replicate traditional firing processes. The results showed that firing temperatures significantly affected internal structures, strength and contraction rates, highlighting optimal firing temperatures for each type of simulant to achieve desired properties.

The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber, considering the effects of slip at the liquid-solid interface, have been analyzed using the phase-field model. By varying the liquid's surface tension and slip parameter, researchers discovered a broad range of dynamic behaviors, from steady states to complex patterns and liquid detachment. The presence of slip accelerated the Rayleigh-Plateau instability and altered the regime of steady states versus dynamics. Furthermore, slip led to the emergence of a new type of instability, as well as a phenomenon where liquid layers could form on fibers with diameters significantly smaller than the critical height for instability in unslippery liquids.

By comparing various star formation rate (SFR) indicators, we can assess their reliability and preferences for specific physical properties of galaxies. Previous studies have highlighted discrepancies between SFR indicators and their potential biases due to a galaxy's physical state. Notably, strong evidence suggests that dust temperature affects SFR indicators in infrared and far-infrared wavelengths, but the extent of this influence remains unclear. By cross-analyzing data from the SINGS database and six far-infrared lines, we have identified Brackett-$\gamma$ as a definitive indicator of SFR, unaffected by dust temperature. Additionally, we have used empirical SFR formulas to develop a unbiased calibration for far-infrared emission, which is preferred over model-derived calibrations that are influenced by dust temperature and mass. By cross-validation, we have observed that empirical SFR formulas derived from optical and near-infrared data are also unaffected by dust temperature, underscoring their reliability as universal SFR indicators.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we thoroughly examine the regional submodules in the tensor categories of the type II quantum subgroups, while the upcoming paper will focus on establishing connections between these regional modules and parabolic subgroups of the quantum group's representation.

We introduce an innovative method to solve the general diffusion equation, providing a thorough mathematical framework for the technique. This approach is inspired by the QSA method, which was developed by Carneiro in 2015 and further refined by Carneiro and Mello in 2017. The novel method establishes a clear connection between the general diffusion equation and the quantum eigenvalue problem, enabling the calculation of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the operator $H$ in relation to the stationary probability density of a $d$-dimensional random walk. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method can be used to determine the critical exponents and functions associated with the operator $H$, which are relevant to various applications, including combinatorial problems and mathematical physics.

This research paper focuses on recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions 
using information from a stylus-based input device. The document begins by outlining 
key challenges involved in processing mathematical input and proposes a novel approach.
Specifically, we analyze how users interact with such systems through their input 
behavior, handwriting patterns, and the temporal dynamics of expression creation.
Additionally, we present a unique dataset consisting of annotated mathematical 
expressions, known as the "MathHand" dataset, which was collected from 30 individuals
using a hand-tracking device. The dataset contains temporal segmentation data along with
relevant spatial characteristics extracted from each segment. Following a detailed
evaluation of various approaches to recognize mathematical expressions, we ultimately
determine that a combination of feature-based methods, enhanced by temporal segmentation 
analysis, yields the most effective performance. Consequently, we have integrated this 
combination into our proposed expression recognition framework. Experimental results 
validate our approach, demonstrating its superior performance on the MathHand dataset 
and showcasing significant progress over existing benchmark results.

This study introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent neural network to predict the median log-frame duration as a function of prior frames. This network is optimised through back-propagation, taking into account the variance of auxiliary frames whose existence is inferred from the output. This median-based approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in modelling the log-frame duration of speech.

Species distribution analysis can be conducted through spatial presence models that account for individual species, multiple species, or a combination of presence-absence and abundance data. The rR package, spOccupancy, is utilized to build and evaluate these models, which are based on hierarchical Bayesian principles and incorporate spatial correlation. The package facilitates model fitting and comparison for single species, allowing for the estimation of species parameters, uncertainty analysis, and prediction of species presence and abundance. Furthermore, the package includes functions for model validation, species selection, and data imputation. Example use cases are provided in the package documentation and supplemented by a comprehensive vignette.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare initiative aims to address this by creating an interactive deep learning system that aids general practitioners in accurately diagnosing skin lesions. This is achieved through a simplified user interface enabling communication with the system, consisting of two components: a differential diagnosis module and a diagnostic confirmation module. The first module provides the top three diagnosis probabilities based on a brief patient description, following which the practitioner selects and provides a biopsy image for the final diagnosis. Employing a training and testing protocol grounded in clinical settings, the system was trained on the publicly available ISIC dataset. Results indicate a 0.40 Area Under the ROC curve for the initial three diagnoses and 0.61 for the final four diagnoses.

To improve the modeling of Type Ia supernovae, we've developed a probabilistic autoencoder tailored to temporal spectrum data. By capturing the intrinsic variability of these events, our method aims to eliminate noise-related biases in the model's parameters. We tested our approach using a model based on recurrent neural networks and found that it effectively identifies the most representative features from multiple spectral measurements. Furthermore, our method allows for the integration of prior knowledge on supernova evolution through the inclusion of a custom-designed variational autoencoder. The results demonstrate that prior knowledge can be leveraged to boost the model's performance. We also explored the influence of different encoding schemes and found that a deep, multi-layered encoder yields the best outcomes.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a dusty star-forming galaxy at a distance of 2.09 billion light-years. The galaxy, which has 10 billion times the sun's mass, is so far away that its light takes over 8 billion years to reach us, and its appearance is obscured by intense dust clouds. The outflow's properties suggest it is driven by the galaxy's active star formation and may be the key to understanding how galaxies like this one grow and develop. The outflow's mass is estimated to be a significant portion of the galaxy's total mass, and its speed is impressive, with estimates ranging from 500 to 1000 kilometers per second. The outflow's shape and direction are also quite extended, with a dusty tail observed in the galaxy's center. The outflow's neutral gas is likely the result of a rapid gas outflow that has had little time to interact with the galaxy's ionizing photons. The observation of this massive outflow and its effects will help scientists better understand the galaxy's growth and development, and the role it plays in the galaxy's evolution. The observation is also consistent with the galaxy's predicted growth and development, and the observed outflow is likely to have a significant impact on the galaxy's future evolution.

We examine how fluid moves into a plume that contains particles distributed throughout it. The plume's topmost point grows at a constant rate, but only if the fluid entering it exceeds a lower boundary rate, known as the entrainment rate, the plume's dynamics change significantly. This study focuses on how the fluid's flow into the plume changes in the presence of these particles, and how their behavior affects the flow. The study uses both theoretical analysis and simulations, placed within a broader framework, to understand this complex process. The results indicate that the fluid's flow into the plume decreases slightly in the presence of the particles, and this effect increases as the particles' behavior becomes more restricted. The study also derives an equation to describe this flow, and validates it using the simulations. The results of the study show that the particles' behavior affects their distribution within the plume, and this effect increases as their movement becomes more restricted. The study also observes that the particles accumulate at the plume's base, creating a layer that affects the fluid's flow into the plume. The study concludes by comparing the fluid's flow into the plume in the presence of the particles to their behavior in other processes, and identifies key differences, including the role of the particles' interaction with each other.

Understanding how diseases spread within complex networks involves moving beyond simple graph models, moving on to more advanced hypergraphs that can capture multi-way relationships. A new framework for analyzing disease transmission on hypergraphs is developed, allowing for the creation of disease models that are tied to the network's underlying structure. Ultimately, this new framework enables the creation of a 'critical threshold' for ending an epidemic, and the work presents a new method for identifying this threshold based on the largest eigenvalue of a related matrix.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of a CrI$_3$ bilayer, reveal the detailed mechanism underlying its spin texture formation. Utilizing an effective Heisenberg model with spin-orbit coupling, researchers find that a unique combination of chirality and Rashba effects contribute to the spin texture in the central layer of the bilayer. Analysis shows that this phenomenon arises from the competition between exchange interactions and spin-orbit coupling that leads to effective sublattice imbalances. Additionally, a finite layer intermixing results in differential effective chirality and Rashba-related impacts on spin polarization in the central layer. These findings demonstrate that controlling exchange interactions' relative strength and spin-orbit coupling can effectively manipulate the spin texture within these materials, opening doors for novel spin technology applications.

To determine how the differential rotation of a solar-type star affects its magnetic behavior, we have developed a comprehensive mean-field dynamo model that takes into account the unique characteristics of rapidly rotating stars. Specifically, we have investigated how the differential rotation of a star rotating at less than half of its maximum rate affects its magnetic behavior. Our results reveal that strong differential rotation can prevent magnetic cycles and promote non-variable magnetic behavior in stars. To achieve magnetic cycles, rotation rates must be within a relatively narrow range, and we observe no evidence of variable magnetic behavior in slowly rotating stars below this range. Our research emphasizes the significance of rotation speed in the magnetic behavior of stars and contributes to the understanding of variable and non-variable magnetic behavior in the field.

We present a novel deep learning approach tailored for K-fan multimodal problem-solving, suitable for a wide range of applications involving multiple inputs and outputs. The proposed framework can be adapted to tackle various challenges, such as generating images from multiple modalities or synthesizing texts based on multiple inputs. The core of our model lies in its key-fan module, which enables efficient multi-modal interactions and enables the model to focus on key information across all input modalities while ignoring redundant details. Additionally, a shared-representation module allows for the generation of common features across all input modalities, enhancing the model's performance by incorporating the shared properties. The model can be trained end-to-end using a shared feature loss that measures the difference between the input modalities and the predicted outputs. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses existing state-of-the-art models for the given applications.

The McMini system, a model checker for multithreaded programs, uses the McCarroll abstract machine to identify potential errors in synchronization or data access. By introducing an automatic invalidation mechanism, McMini enhances the traditional McChung-Kuo model checker and a previous McMini prototype. This improved version handles non-interruptible blocks, arbitrary thread scheduling, and data corruptions, making it more robust. Additionally, McMini allows for the automatic detection of valid program paths through reachability analysis.

In 2020, misinformation circulating on WhatsApp contributed to public disorder in several countries, prompting the platform to limit forwarding capabilities for individual messages to 5 recipients. Our study assesses the effectiveness of these restrictions in reducing the spread of misinformation, as evidenced in Mexico following the COVID-19 pandemic. We discovered that targeted public health misinformation propagated rapidly among close networks, often reaching 90% of possible individuals within 4.2 degrees of separation. Conversely, unfettered messages traveled further (5.5 degrees) and reached fewer people (40% of possible individuals). Notably, the new limits reduced misinformation dissemination by 75%, as detected by users' self-reported data. Users complained about these limits, with 35% of surveyed Mexican WhatsApp users opposing them, claiming they would increase misinformation spread. In reality, the changes appears to have concurrently decreased misinformation and user complaints.

We're analyzing populations that follow a general super-critical branching model, where individual members give birth to new individuals at random times according to a specified distribution. The first generation arises through independent births from a initial set of individuals. A key aspect of this population is tracked through the frequencies of individual genes passed down through generations. The system's evolution is complex due to the intricate timing of new member arrivals and their parentage. The frequencies of individual genes converge over time toward one of two possible endpoints - either the population's extinction or its never-ending growth - located on a specific manifold within a higher-dimensional space. These frequencies can be understood through a complex dimensionally higher approximation that reduces as dimension decreases. The difficulty of working with these frequencies is overcome by deriving a simpler, more manageable dimension that still captures the population's core behavior, similar to previous methods for sub-critical and critical branching models. The simplicity of these dimensions comes at a cost of introducing an additional level of approximation error. The methods developed here can also be applied to simulate the distribution of individual genes among a fixed number of population members. The error associated with these simulations can be quantified and specific conditions identified that allow these estimates to converge toward accurate results as more data is collected.

The primary goal of spoofing countermeasure systems in speaker verification is to identify and neutralize the effects of speech forgery, which typically involves prioritizing genuine speech over impersonated speech. We introduce an improved system that utilizes a weighted average of activation values from the fully connected layers to achieve this goal, allowing it to effectively counter speech impersonation. We also detail why this approach was necessary and evaluate its performance using the SAD dataset from the VoxCeleb1 dataset, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing systems.

We've analyzed various mechanisms of inflation that arise from supersymmetric effective field theories, featuring complex line operators on a K3 surface with specific divisors. By examining the global symmetries of these theories, we've identified possible inflationary scenarios and their associated charges, then discussed non-Abelian anomalies within the context of these models. Additionally, we've explored the possibilities of combining multiple inflationary mechanisms and modeled the dynamics of SUSY inflationary models using modular forms, with specific examples involving heterotic string theory constructions.

We examine the phenomenon of asymmetry in photon pair correlations, a notable characteristic of phenomena originating from decay processes. This asymmetry can serve as a distinct marker for identifying such decay processes. Our research focuses on three types of sources: those induced by spontaneous decay, coherent sources, and thermal sources. By analyzing the square modulus of the correlation function $|g^{(2)}(\tau)|$, we find that only sources from decay processes display a distinct asymmetry. Consequently, measuring this asymmetry may offer a method to differentiate between various source types. Furthermore, we identify that coherent sources can mimic the correlation pattern of decay processes through a balance between source rate and decay rate. Nevertheless, a distinct difference persists in correlation function behavior for large $\tau$.

Identifying and manipulating the Josephson effect in quantum devices relies heavily on a thorough understanding of the radiation characteristics of these devices. To achieve this, we utilize advanced nanoscale terahertz spectroscopy techniques, combining both optical and microwave methods. By applying this approach to a study of a CPW resonator, we're able to derive precise information about the device's electrical properties, matching existing simulation data with remarkable accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability to image this macroscopic object at a nanoscale with both optical and microwave stimuli, offering potential future applications in quantum circuit characterization and fault analysis.

We demonstrate that the real axis can be divided into countably infinite Borel sets. This is accomplished by constructing a sequence of continuous functions that map the real axis to the integers, and then utilizing the Borel hierarchy to create the desired partition.

This study examines the impact of innovative investment tactics on the profitability of pre-existing strategies in financial markets. A novel approach, known as Smart Money, is introduced which operates according to rules akin to those of Imitation Timing, a concept first proposed by Brock and Scheinkman in 2006. Analysis, grounded in agent-based modeling, reveals that Smart Money can replicate the results of Timing, yielding similar profits in financial markets. However, when incorporating multiple tactics, including Herd Behavior and a trend-following strategy, it is discovered that Smart Money diminishes the returns of timing-based investment methods. Consequently, this research suggests that the adoption of innovative investment tactics by institutional investors can negatively affect the effectiveness of timing-based strategies employed by individual investors.

A fundamental security requirement for network security monitoring is detecting malicious traffic, and a specific method, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), does this by analyzing packet data. Although DPI is widely used, it has significant limitations: every new traffic pattern needs to be manually programmed, making it inflexible and inefficient. A more modern approach, called application flow analysis, uses machine learning or statistical methods to identify patterns in network traffic, and some frameworks achieve this without custom code. One such example, Suricata, includes a Bayesian classifier called Hunt, which identifies malicious traffic in this way. In a study, researchers examined the effectiveness of this approach and discovered that changing certain traffic properties could evade classification, effectively making them undetectable. To mitigate this, researchers proposed two methods, one of which significantly improved Hunt's robustness.

Two-dimensional ferromagnetic materials are in high demand due to their potential for supporting the fastest possible propagation of spin waves. However, their magnetic response can be severely impacted by the surrounding environment, particularly if they interface with materials that have unusual properties like superconductivity. To better understand this influence, we have explored the effects of pairing and ferromagnetism that occur on the surface of superconductors, focusing on the boundary between the superconductor and the ferromagnet. By modeling this interaction, we have discovered that the characteristics of the superconductor can significantly alter the available frequency range and mobility of magnetic waves in the ferromagnet, potentially limiting these waves' ability to cross the interface. This suggests that magnetic waves can be effectively gated or blocked by the superconductor's influence on their frequency. Therefore, interface engineering that accounts for the properties of gate materials like superconductors could offer a novel strategy for managing magnetic waves' behavior.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, several challenges persist in this method: (1) users' devices might not match the model's parameters, resulting in communication inefficiencies, (2) clients may refrain from participating due to model distribution discrepancies, and (3) the server may find it difficult to develop effective models across diverse clients. This study introduces advancements over conventional federated learning in audio classification environments, tackling the aforementioned hurdles: (1) we devise a novel method to instantly define layer parameters using global attributes, eliminating initialization requirements, (2) we develop a technique to instantly generalize from local to global parameters, ensuring smooth interactions between users, and (3) we propose a universal model capable of instantly incorporating client-specific features. Experimental results demonstrate that our method breaks through inter-client feature differences and outperforms traditional federated learning in two distinct audio classification scenarios.

Recent breakthroughs in multi-partite entanglement have sparked a need to examine the quantum entanglement phenomenon in high-dimensional systems. Specifically, we propose a method for measuring a high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state using an array of optical fibers, a process which can be realized with current technology. Our approach relies on a multi-step process involving the selection of entangled photons, manipulation of the photons' modes, and collision-based detection of the entangled states. Our study shows that high-dimensional GHZ states can be efficiently measured with minimal error rates when the number of entangled parts exceeds 10. Moreover, our research predicts a non-zero quantum gain for multi-partite entanglement in high-dimensional systems, opening avenues for future research and development in high-dimensional quantum information processing and research.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces. Due to the high convergence rate and computational efficiency of the proposed low-complexity method, it can be repeatedly utilized for simultaneous estimation of both the channel and the IRS reflection matrix. The latter is achieved through successive reflection phase optimization. The findings reveal that the estimated values closely resemble the actual values, resulting in negligible performance degradation. The experiments further demonstrate the robustness and speed of the estimation process can be enhanced by increasing the number of training symbols and deepening the subchannel sparsity, respectively.

This study analyzes the relationship between local online news coverage of COVID-19 and the actual pandemic metrics in the United States from March to November 2020. Utilizing a diverse national sample of 323 areas, we tracked both the volume and tone of local news coverage alongside COVID-19 cases and deaths. Our results reveal that areas with more coverage of COVID-19 actually experienced fewer cases and deaths, while the tone of that coverage was also associated with lower mortality rates. Furthermore, local news audiences were more likely to experience deaths from COVID-19 if the news tone was more negative, suggesting a potential link between audience exposure to local news and their vulnerability to the pandemic.

We developed a novel sequence-to-sequence model based on reinforcement learning to resolve the limitation of perceptive restriction in the counting task popularized by Kahananukkunen et al. (2018). Our model utilizes the generative model framework, training a generator to produce correct sentence representations and a discriminator to verify their accuracy. We combined this framework with attention and dynamic list length input to create a model that can efficiently learn from small datasets. We tested our model and a comparison model that incorporates additional training with the same data, both with and without memory augmentation. The results indicate that our model outperforms the comparison model, achieving a perfect score on the development set and 97.5% accuracy on the test set. Additionally, our model demonstrates computational efficiency by requiring significantly fewer training steps.

Bloom filters provide efficient approximations to membership testing, typically achieving 100% accuracy with filters significantly larger than the compressed version. Cuckoo filters offer an improved alternative, eliminating false positives at the cost of increased storage and processing time. Xor Filters presented in this research demonstrate a compromise, providing rapid membership testing with near BHT sizes and a low false positive rate, surpassing CUK efficiency while eliminating its false positives. Additionally, Xor Filters frequently reach 100% accuracy, exceeding both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in various scenarios.

This note expands on the talk delivered at the conference "Convexity and a conjecture of Gromov" held in June 2021. It covers the content of the talk, which explored connections between convex geometry and complex geometry in relation to Gromov's distance conjecture. The talk initially established a correspondence between certain properties in convex geometry and in K-stability for smooth toric varieties. It then delved into the distality of cones associated with toric varieties, proving that this distality is equivalent to the stability of the associated manifold. A key step in this distivity analysis involved demonstrating that it could be quantified over arbitrary non-degenerate embedded smooth closed convex cones. Furthermore, a thorough examination was conducted on the extremal smooth distal closed convex cones, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between these and the smooth delocalized K-stable manifold pairs.

This paper presents an innovative method to extract and analyze market trend signals, leveraging the sequential flow of trade data. To achieve this, we introduce two key indices: the leading and lagging directional strength, both of which are derived from the price-time-share sequence of trades and incorporate predictions from future trade data. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of these indices by comparing their performance to established signals, such as those based on trading volumes and technical analysis indicators, when predicting stock price movements. Notably, the lead and lag indices have shown superior performance in a variety of statistical tests and have the potential to improve existing methods by incorporating the influence of future trade data and a more comprehensive analysis approach.

This work introduces FLVoogd, a refined federated learning framework, designed to enhance security and protect user privacy. Specifically, FLVoogd incorporates advanced measures: 1) a sophisticated attack detection system, 2) a strategic client hiring process, and 3) a dynamic model updating mechanism. By integrating these features, FLVoogd effectively countersinsidious inner and outer attacks, and also mitigates the influence of malicious clients on the learning process. After thorough testing on various configurations, our results demonstrate that FLVoogd offers substantial improvements over existing federated learning protocols.

We successfully integrated optical flow prediction into an end-to-end autonomous driving system, closing the gap between simulated performance and real-world results. In this study, we examined how to bridge the simulation-to-reality gap by using multi-scale optical flow estimation from simulated images to guide real-world image processing. Our approach leverages a two-part system: the first generates simulated ground-truth maps for real-world images, and the second utilizes these maps to guide the processing of the same images. Both components were based on convolutional neural networks. Our results showed that the optical flow estimation could effectively translate from simulated to real-world settings, and when combined with a mapping algorithm, it could significantly improve the real-world performance and stability of the autonomous driving system.

Significant breakthroughs have greatly increased the use of AI-generated deepfakes, with deepfake generation methods now capable of producing entirely realistic videos, even when the origin material is drawn from TV shows, movies, and video games. Despite being generally available, deepfake creation tools are still inaccessible to the average user, with even the most advanced methods requiring sophisticated technical expertise. A key hurdle lies in preparing the original 2D images for deepfake generation, a process that can be extremely time-consuming. This research aims to address these challenges by developing user-friendly deepfake creation tools and exploring the intricacies of deepfake detection, with a particular focus on the key factors that contribute to resilient deepfake discrimination.

The difference in transit observables due to different models of gas solubility and chemistry in exoplanetary atmospheres allows us to determine the presence or absence of a liquid envelope around an exoplanet. By analyzing the observables of K2-18 b, our current data and previously published results reveal that the transit depth at 1.52 micrometers is higher than expected from atmospheric models without a liquid envelope, indicating the need for one. However, the required liquid envelope opacity to explain the observed transit depth differences is relatively low, suggesting that the envelope is likely shallow. Additionally, our analysis shows that the atmospheric pressure at which carbon dioxide condenses is higher than its equilibrium pressure, and that the radius of rocky planets in the system is likely greater than 1.30 times the radius of Earth.

A significant goal in artificial neural networks is to mimic biological synapse dynamics learning processes, despite previous studies that have introduced unrealistic conditions such as simultaneous pre- and post-synaptic activity. We address this challenge by developing an unsupervised, spike-based learning algorithm for spiking neural networks that aligns with biological principles, assuming synapses update locally following individual post-synaptic neuron activity. The algorithm utilizes a novel learning rule that we validated through simulations on diverse network architectures, demonstrating its efficacy and efficiency. Furthermore, our results highlight the substantial differences between synapse update mechanisms and their impacts on learning performance.

This paper outlines the performance of various models in an unprecedented 'out-of-category' (OoC) challenge. Unlike standard classification tasks where datasets are consistent in distribution, the OoC challenge exposes models to unanticipated input sources. Our research evaluates classification models when faced with unforeseen data variants, leveraging existing literature on out-of-distribution detection and post-decision uncertainty analysis to measure OoC performance. Our investigation addresses two primary questions: how do models behave when confronted with novel data types, and which models exhibit enhanced robustness against unforeseen inputs. Our study differs from existing research by assessing OoC performance across a wide range of input sources rather than a single unexpected category. While a model may excel on a particular OoC dataset, it may struggle with novel data types, and our work simulates this scenario using images from the ImageNet dataset substituted for labels in the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our findings indicate a model's performance in one OoC scenario does not guarantee its effectiveness in another, and our data suggests that using Bayesian neural networks to estimate output uncertainty provides a viable approach to measuring OoC performance. Furthermore, our research highlights the potential benefits and limitations of training models on multiple data sources to boost their robustness against unforeseen inputs, and our data suggests that utilizing expert knowledge to select the most relevant training data can improve a model's OoC robustness.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states, which are often difficult to compute directly. By utilizing generalized polynomial chaos expansions, researchers can approximate random solution trajectories with a high degree of accuracy, even when general uncertainty types are involved. Although these expansions can be computationally expensive to implement, a recent method allows for the efficient construction of verification certificates, which can ensure the correctness and accuracy of the results obtained from the approximations. This framework is then applied to verify the results of approximating semi-active suspension systems with uncertain factors.

We introduce a novel approach to detecting sequential changes in data streams, capable of handling multiple shifts at various times and accommodating both known and unknown change points. Our algorithm, designed for online use, processes data in real-time and leverages partial observability by only requiring partial data stream knowledge to function effectively. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that a modified version of the SGI* algorithm outperforms other methods on partial observability and surpasses or competes with others on fully observable datasets. Our work has practical applications in areas like anomaly detection and monitoring dynamic systems to minimize losses. The code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.pitt.edu/nithin-krishna/sgi-adapt.

We've obtained high-resolution spectra of eight dwarf galaxy globular clusters, allowing us to determine their metal content and study the birth histories of these galaxies through the process of star creation. This research utilizes an advanced model that accounts for star creation histories and relies on the analysis of rare, unique stars. Our findings indicate that about seven billion years ago, these dwarf galaxies began forming in a manner consistent with calm star creation histories, producing stars at an steady rate over time. However, our data also reveals evidence that another set of dwarf galaxy globular clusters, including those similar to omega Centauri, were formed through a different process involving chaotic star creation. This distinction leads to significantly distinct chemical properties, with the calm star creation group displaying uniform metal content and the chaotic group exhibiting greater variability in both metal content and star creation rates. Furthermore, our model indicates that the calm star creation group's uniform metal content is a result of their similar birth times, with the calm and chaotic groups separated by at least 1.5 billion years. Our data also suggests that the calm star creation group's star creation rates peaked around ten times faster than current rates, with the calm and chaotic groups experiencing differing levels of star creation fluctuations. This research indicates that the calm star creation group's compact cluster star creation patterns are a result of their early formation within the dwarf galaxy, with their uniform metal content a result of their shared birth time.

We establish a refined version of the Borel construction for finite truncations of spaces subject to actions by profinite groups, thereby laying a foundational role in establishing an equivalence between the homotopy theory of these spaces and that of spectra. This idea is further developed by exploring the relationship between classifying spaces and group cohomology, where we demonstrate that the resulting theory corresponds to non-canonical graded equivariant cohomology theories. This work also leads to the creation of a theory of profinite group actions on spaces that we term'strict'. This notion solidifies the relationship between the theory of strict profinite group actions and homotopy theory of spectra, where we prove that functors preserving this'strictness' structure establish an equivalence with functors from the category of strict profinite group actions on spaces to the category of spectra. This result bears resemblance to Borel's construction in that preserving the'strictness' structure is analogous to preserving the 'free action' structure when considering the Borel construction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any strict profinite group action on a space can be reinterpreted as an action on a spectrum, where we term this equivalence 'pivotal'. This notion solidifies the relationship between the theory of pivotal profinite group actions on spaces and theory of spectra with a pivotal automorphism. Lastly, we establish an equivalence between any of these three theories: the theory of strict profinite group actions on spaces, the theory of pivotal profinite group actions

Accurate training of document extraction models requires a substantial collection of visually complex documents, each annotated with precise extraction specifications. However, manually annotating data for these tasks is extremely time-consuming, making it a major expense in the machine learning pipeline. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach that combines two advanced techniques: CLONET for efficient data collection and sequential transformer for task execution. CLONET enables the creation of high-quality training datasets by mimicking human annotation processes, while the sequential transformer model leverages attention mechanisms to achieve superior performance. Our research involves an in-depth analysis of the CLONET methodology, followed by a detailed evaluation of its performance in reducing data annotation costs and improving model results.

The EuS/InAs interface has garnered interest due to potential applications in binary neuromorphics and quantum computing. To examine the electronic properties of this interface, we employed ab initio method to calculate its behavior when the interface's configuration changed. Using slabs with 14 Å van der Waals separation, we discovered that the interface energy displayed a notable resonance at 0.35 eV below the Fermi level. Furthermore, the results of our calculations indicated that the resonance is comprised of states localized in the EuS monolayer and InAs substrate. Additionally, we found that the effective mass of the InAs dipole moment exhibited an upside-down trend as the InAs monolayer's dipole moment aligned with the external field. The InAs dipole moment's effective mass behaved oppositely in the two studied configurations.

We present an efficient classification system for Borel Wadge classes, which builds upon Moore's recursive construction of Borel Wadge classes. Our classification system enhances Moore's method by employing recursive strategies that facilitate construction of codes without requiring transfinite induction, thus making it more computationally accessible. Additionally, we demonstrate that this classification system can be computed effectively using only $\Pi^1_2$-many computations, whereas Moore's original method relies on a specific level of infinite ordinal for computation purposes.

Deep learning models continue to experience an upswing in their size, leading to elevated training costs. The cost can be mitigated through pruning, a post-model-training process that spares results' accuracy. Nevertheless, current pruning techniques are inefficient as they usually eliminate entire neurons, overlook spatial correlations within data, and discard model features. This paper introduces ClickTrain, a innovative method that integrates pruning with a new technique called "fine-grained re-growth," allowing for precise model reduction. ClickTrain's re-growth process regrows model sections with high prediction confidence on input data, thus ensuring the model's accuracy is unaffected. ClickTrain's worth has been proven through experiments where it outperforms traditional pruning methods by up to 4 times on various models, such as MobileNetV2 and ResNet-50, with model sizes reduced by as much as 72% without compromising results' accuracy.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the distributive complete Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model semantics.

The incorporation of neutron star information in gravitational wave models enhances their complexity, but also offers additional insights that can improve the accuracy of inferring binary parameters and physical properties, such as the binary masses and spin parameters. A deep learning method is developed to analyze the characteristics of binary neutron star and black hole mergers that produce detectable gravitational waves, with simulations indicating that a multi-layered neural network can accurately distinguish between these events, with an optimal accuracy of 99.98% for 10 iterations. Furthermore, this network can estimate the binary masses and spin parameters of the compact objects, with correlations similar to those found in other methods, including parameters derived from quasi-local spin estimates that are computed offline. When applied to neutron star-black hole mergers, this approach can predict the properties of these events, such as the final neutron star mass, with estimated mass errors of less than 0.05 solar masses.
